en: Kāmandaki Nītisāra, First Chapter.
The Chapter on the Conquest of the Senses:
Victorious is that illustrious lord of the earth, the divine wielder of the rod of punishment, by whose power the world abides on the eternal path. (1)
In a lineage of many great-souled ancestors, like sages,
he became renowned on earth as one who never accepted gifts.
Like the fire Jātavedas in his brilliance, he, the best among those who know the Vedas,
has studied the four Vedas with great skill as if they were a single Veda.
By the thunderbolt of his sorcery, which possessed the blazing splendor of a diamond, the glorious and well-jointed Mount Nanda fell uprooted from its base. (4)
Alone, by the power of his mantras, he who was like the wielder of the spear (Śiva) through his might brought the earth to Candragupta, that moon among men.
Salutations to that creator Viṣṇugupta, who extracted the nectar of the science of ethics from the great ocean of the Arthaśāstra. (6)
Because of his vision, he who is well-seeing and has reached the further shore of all sciences,
[composed this work] which is concise yet meaningful, out of his love for the royal science.
Regarding the acquisition and protection of land toward the lord of the earth, we shall set forth whatever [instruction] is the opinion of those who know the science of kingship. (8)
The king was the cause of this world's prosperity, as esteemed by the elders as the moon is for the ocean, generating delight for the eyes. (9)
If there were no king who is a proper leader, then the subjects here would perish like a ship without a helmsman in the ocean. (10)
The subjects regard a king who is righteous, devoted to protection, and a true conqueror of enemy cities as they do Prajāpati himself. ||11||
O Queen, protection depends upon the king; the livelihood of the people depends upon protection.
For if their livelihood is cut off, this world does not truly live, even though it breathes. (12)
The lord of the earth is the support of all beings like the rain-cloud; for even when the rain-cloud fails, one may survive, but not when the king fails. 13.
The king protects the subjects, and they in turn cause the monarch to prosper.
Protection is superior to mere prosperity; for if that protection fails, even other virtues, though existing, are as if non-existent.
A king who proceeds according to justice [protects] both himself and his subjects.
He binds himself with the threefold aim; otherwise, he is surely destroyed. ||15||
Through righteousness, King Vaijavana enjoyed the earth for a long time;
and through unrighteousness, Nahuṣa fell to the subterranean realm.
Therefore, placing Dharma at the forefront, a king should strive for his own welfare;
through Dharma his kingdom prospers, and the fruit of his prosperity is sweet.
The sovereign, the minister, the realm, the fortification, the treasury, the army, and the ally—this much is called a kingdom, which depends upon both strength and intelligence. (18)
Having taken hold of a powerful being and having discerned the way out through the intellect, one should strive, ever-exerting oneself, for the attainment of these seven limbs. (19)
The acquisition of wealth by righteous means, its preservation, its increase, and its bestowal upon worthy recipients—this fourfold conduct constitutes the duty of a king. (20)
Endowed with policy and prowess, and being well-exerted, one should contemplate prosperity;
for discipline is the root of policy, and discipline is the certainty derived from the treatises. ||21||
Discipline is indeed the conquest of the senses; one endowed with that attains the scripture.
For the meanings of the scripture become clear to one who is devoted to that, and from that, prosperity follows. 22.
Learning, wisdom, fortitude, skill, eloquence, retentiveness, energy, oratorical power, steadfastness, and endurance of calamities and suffering. ||23||
Power, purity, friendliness, generosity, truthfulness, gratitude, noble birth, good character, and self-control—these are the qualities that cause prosperity. (24)
First, the king should establish himself in discipline;
then his ministers, then his servants, then his sons, and finally his subjects. (25)
A king whose subjects are ever devoted, who is intent on protecting his people, and whose self is disciplined, indeed attains abundant prosperity. (26)
One should bring under control, by means of the goad of knowledge, the elephant of the senses which runs wild in the forest of sense-objects and causes great distress.
Through effort, the self presides over the mind for the sake of objects;
from the conjunction of the self and the mind, activity arises. (28)
Driven by greed for the bait of sense-objects, the mind impels the senses;
one should restrain it with effort, for when it is conquered, the senses are conquered. (29)
Consciousness, the heart, the mind, the intellect, and the faculty of thought are all identical;
by means of these, the self performs here both engagement and withdrawal. (30)
Dharma and adharma, pleasure and pain, as well as desire and aversion, effort, cognition, and mental impressions—these are declared to be the marks of the self. (31)
The non-simultaneity of cognitions is stated to be the mark of the mind;
its function is proclaimed to be the formation of volitional constructs regarding various objects. (32)
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech—this is the collection of the sense organs (indriya). ||33||
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth; and excretion, sexual pleasure, grasping, movement, and speech are their respective functions. ||34||
The self (ātman) and the mind (manas) are called the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) by those who know that [science].
From these two, together with effort, volition (saṅkalpa) arises. (35)
The self, the intellect, and the sense organs are called the external instruments;
its accomplishment is proclaimed to arise through volition and determination. (36)
For both of these instruments arise immediately following effort;
therefore, by restraining effort, one should cultivate the state of mindlessness. (37)
Thus, by restraining himself through his own self by means of his capacity for action, the king, who discerns what is right and wrong, should act for his own welfare. (38)
How indeed can he who is not even capable of subduing his own single mind conquer the earth bounded by the oceans? (39)
With his heart captivated by sense objects that are fleeting and devoid of flavor at their conclusion, the king goes to his palace like an elephant drawn away from its herd.
For a king whose vision is blinded by sense objects, becoming attached to improper actions, brings upon himself a calamity that produces fierce fear. (41)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—each one of these leads to the realization of destruction. 42.
Pure, feeding on sprouts of young grass, and capable of leaping over great distances,
the deer seeks his own destruction through his greed for the hunter's song.
An elephant, whose form resembles the king of mountains and who playfully uproots trees,
goes to his tethering post due to the delusion caused by the touch of a female elephant.
One whose eyes are enticed by the light of a glistening lamp flame undoubtedly meets death, like a moth suddenly falling [into the flame]. (45)
For even though he dwells far away, moving in fathomless water,
the fish, by tasting the iron bait with its meat, brings about his own death.
The honey-bee, greedy for fragrance and thirsting for the nectar of the gift,
approached the jhanañjhana sounds of the elephant's ears, which were difficult to traverse.
Even individually, the sense objects are like poison;
how indeed could one who indulges in all five equally remain secure? (48)
One who has mastered himself should enjoy the objects of the senses at the proper time, having set aside his single-minded devotion [to them];
for pleasure is indeed the fruit of wealth, and its prosperity is in vain if that [pleasure] is withheld.
For those whose minds are intensely attached to gazing upon the face of their beloved,
their youthful charms vanish along with their falling tears.
From dharma comes wealth; from wealth, desire; and from desire, the arising of the fruit of happiness.
He who does not practice these two through proper means destroys himself by destroying them. (51)
Even the mere name "woman" is heart-gladdening and truly agitates the mind; how much more so the sight of her, whose eyebrows are made to dance by her playful charms? (52)
Skilled in private dalliance, speaking with soft and faltering words, and possessing eyes with reddened corners, what impassioned man would she not delight? (53)
A woman inevitably makes even the mind of a sage full of passion, just as the twilight makes the lunar orb bright and radiant. (54)
For even great men are shattered by women who delight the mind and move with slow grace, just as mountains are split apart by waters.
Hunting, gambling, and drinking are censured for kings;
yet calamities arising from these were seen even among the Pāṇḍus, Nala, and the Vṛṣṇis.
Lust, anger, greed, elation, pride, and intoxication—one should cast off this group of six; when these are abandoned, O King, the monarch shall be happy.
King Dāṇḍakya [perished] through lust, Janamejaya through anger, the royal sage Aila through greed, and the asura Vātāpi through pride. (58)
The Rākṣasa Paulastya through pride, and King Dambhodbhava through arrogance—these indeed met their destruction because they relied upon the group of six internal enemies. (59)
Having cast off the group of six enemies, the son of Jamadagni, who had conquered his senses,
and the highly fortunate Ambarīṣa both enjoyed the earth for a long time.
In this section on association with those advanced in learning:
Having cultivated virtue and worldly prosperity here through diligent service to the virtuous, one who has restrained the senses should properly perform service to the guru. (61)
Association with a teacher is for the sake of the scriptures; the scripture leads to the increase of discipline.
A king disciplined by learning does not falter in times of distress.
A king who serves the elderly is esteemed by the virtuous;
even when urged by those of evil conduct, he does not engage in improper deeds.
Taking up his arts properly day by day, the lord of the earth increases like the moon moving through the bright fortnight.
For a king who has conquered his senses and follows the path of righteous conduct,
his fortunes blaze forth and his glories touch the heavens.
Thus the king, endowed with discipline and guided by policy, practicing that conduct honored by gods among men,
ascended to the radiant station of prosperity.
His head was as lofty as the great jewel-mountain.
For this earthly nature, by its very essence, exists apart from worldly ways;
one should therefore forcibly unite it with discipline.
In the increase of policy, discipline is the precursor. ||67||
One who is thoroughly disciplined attains the state of being worthy of service by kings; discipline is their ornament,
like an elephant in rut whose trunk moves gently as it extends its gift.
Like a noble elephant, he shines through his discipline. ||68||
A guru is served for the sake of acquiring knowledge,
and the knowledge thus heard leads to the wisdom of the great-souled ones;
for the thoughts of the wise follow what has been heard by the Creator.
Without doubt, they become truly beneficial for one's welfare. ||69||
Having served a true guru with great skill and purity, being intent on following his instructions for the sake of spiritual prosperity,
one indeed becomes augmented by discipline.
He is capable of attaining the status of a king and of achieving peace. ||70||
For enemies bring even one who is unwilling under their control through diligence, if he delights in lack of discipline;
whereas one who has taken refuge in a treasury of learning and discipline—
Even in its most minute form, it never suffers defeat anywhere. ||71||
The Second Chapter:
The Classification of Sciences.
The king [should study] Ānvīkṣikī, Trayī, Vārtā, and Daṇḍanīti.
One who is endowed with discipline should contemplate [this] together with those who possess that knowledge and are engaged in those practices. ||1||
Logic, the three Vedas, economics, and the eternal science of government—these four indeed are the branches of knowledge for the welfare and security of embodied beings. (2)
The three Vedas, commerce, and the science of government—these, O men, are indeed the three branches of knowledge;
this which is considered Ānvīkṣikī is merely a subdivision of the triple Veda itself. (3)
Economics and the science of government—these two are established as the branches of knowledge;
for the world is primarily concerned with material welfare, the disciples of the preceptor of the gods [were thus instructed]. (4)
"The science of government alone is knowledge," such is the established doctrine of Auśanas;
for within it, the undertakings of all sciences are firmly established. (5)
"These four alone are the sciences"—this is our teacher's view;
they are established separately for the sake of individual accomplishment, and upon them the world is dependent. (6)
The knowledge of the self is found in Ānvīkṣikī; dharma and adharma reside in the Trayī; profit and loss are in Vārtā; and policy and its opposite are in Daṇḍanīti. (7)
They declare that *ānvīkṣikī*, *trayī*, and *vārtā* are the true sciences;
yet even they are not truly real when there is a collapse of *daṇḍanīti*.
When the science of government is properly presided over by a leader, then the remaining sciences are correctly cultivated by those who possess knowledge. (9)
The social classes and the stages of life are established upon these sciences;
by protecting them, the king shares in the merit of their dharma.
Ānvīkṣikī is the science of the self (ātmavidyā), so called because it involves the investigation (īkṣaṇa) of pleasure and pain;
by means of it, one who investigates the true nature of reality casts off both joy and sorrow. (11)
The three Vedas, known by the names Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, are remembered as the Trayī.
One who abides in the Trayī according to the prescribed rule attains both worlds. (12)
The Vedas with their four auxiliary limbs, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya, the Dharmaśāstra, and the Purāṇa—all this is called the Trayī. ||13||

Cattle-rearing, agriculture, and trade constitute the livelihood (vārtā) for those who subsist by such means. One who is successful through this livelihood does not rightly encounter the fear of lack of sustenance.
Self-restraint is called *daṇḍa*; because the king abides in that [restraint], he is called *daṇḍa*. His policy is *daṇḍanīti*, and it is called *nīti* because of his leading [others]. (15)
By means of that [science], may the lord of the earth protect himself and the remaining sciences;
for sciences are beneficial to the world, and it is the lord of the earth who protects them. 16.
One of noble intellect should thoroughly understand the four aims of human life through these sciences;
know that this is the "science-ness" of these sciences, for the root *vid* is etymologically defined as "to know. (17)
The section on the system of castes and stages of life:
Sacrifice, study, and charity, performed according to the scriptures, are declared to be the common duty for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. (18)
Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts from the pure—these three means of livelihood have been declared by the sages for one of the highest caste. (19)
Living by the sword and the protection of living beings are the livelihoods of a king;
cattle-rearing, agriculture, and trade are recorded as the livelihoods of a Vaiśya. (20)
The duty of the Śūdra is the service of the twice-born in their proper order;
his pure livelihood consists of that service, as well as the work of artisans and wandering performers. (21)
Dwelling with the guru, service to the sacred fire, Vedic study, observance of vows, bathing at the three times of day, living on alms, and remaining with the guru until death. ||22||
In the absence of these, [one may seek refuge] with the son of the guru or likewise with a fellow student;
or, by choice, one may change one's stage of life, for the specific duty of a celibate student is his own dharma.

Wearing a girdle, with matted hair or shaven head, and carrying a staff, he should take refuge under a teacher until the completion of his studies; or, according to his desire, he may proceed to another stage of life.
The performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice and living by one's own duties; sexual union with a virtuous wife at the proper time, except on the sacred festival days (*parvan*). (25)
Worship of the gods, ancestors, and guests; compassion for the distressed;
and abiding by the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti—this is the duty of the householder. (26)
Wearing matted hair, maintaining the sacred fire, sleeping on the ground, wearing deerskins, dwelling in the forest, and subsisting on water, roots, wild rice, and fruits. ||27||
Abstaining from accepting gifts, bathing three times a day, the observance of vows, and the worship of gods and guests—this is the dharma of the forest-dweller. (28)
The renunciation of all undertakings, subsisting on alms, dwelling at the foot of trees, possessionlessness, freedom from malice, and equanimity toward all living beings. ||29||
Embracing both the pleasant and the unpleasant, remaining unchanging in the face of pleasure and pain, purity both internal and external, restraint of speech, and the observance of vows; ||30||
The withdrawal of all the senses, concentration, application to meditation, and the complete purification of one's being— this is called the duty of the wandering mendicant.

Non-violence, speech that is pleasant and true, truthfulness, purity, compassion, and forbearance are said to be the common dharma for both those belonging to the social orders (varṇas) and those bearing the marks of religious stages (liṅgas). ||32||
This dharma leads to the infinity of heaven for all those belonging to the castes and those bearing the marks of religious orders;
in its absence, however, this world would meet its destruction through the confusion of classes.
The king is the one who properly sets all of this in motion;
in his absence there is the destruction of Dharma, and in its absence, the ruin of the world. (34)
Endowed with the conduct of the castes and stages of life, knowing the distinctions between castes and stages, and being the protector of the castes and stages, the king shares in all the worlds. 35.
The Section on the Majesty of Punishment: Since the self-possessed king sustains both worlds, he should therefore properly wield punishment over his subjects like one who holds a staff. (36)
With a harsh punishment the king causes agitation; with a mild one he is held in contempt. Therefore, a king who applies appropriate punishment is praised. (37)
The king's punishment, when applied according to the law, quickly increases the three goals of life;
however, if administered unjustly, it would provoke even those dwelling in the forest.

Punishment should be administered in accordance with worldly custom and sacred law so as not to cause alarm, for this leads to prosperity; from causing alarm arises unrighteousness, and from that comes the ruin of the king. (39)
In a world where paths have diverged due to mutual predation, the law of the fish prevails in the absence of punishment, leading to total destruction. (40)
This world, which is without a protector and is being forcibly submerged in hell by desire, greed, and the like, is held back by the king through his rod of punishment. (41)
This world, by its very nature, is enslaved by sense objects and is greedy for the wives and wealth of others;
yet it is upon the eternal path followed by the virtuous that [one must proceed].
It proceeds, oppressed by the fear of punishment.
In this world, which is largely subject to the application of punishment, one who abides within the bounds of fixed moral objects and follows a virtuous conduct is difficult to find;
for even one who is emaciated, crippled, diseased, or afflicted with pain [is often disregarded].
Even a woman of noble family submits to her husband out of fear of punishment. ||43||
Thus, one who has mastered the subject matter, follows the path of the scriptures,
and is self-controlled, governs his subjects through the science of punishment so that they proceed upon the attained path without ever falling away from it again.
Just as rivers enter the ocean, so do all prosperities enter him.
The Third Chapter: On the Establishment of Conduct.
The lord of the earth, wielding punishment over all beings like a staff-bearer, [should act thus].
He should personally favor his subjects, just like Prajāpati himself. ||1||
Truthful speech, compassion, generosity, and the protection of the distressed who approach for help—such is the association with the virtuous; it is beneficial and the vow of the noble person. (2)
As if possessed by a profound sorrow centered upon that [suffering], and filled with supreme compassion, one should rescue the wretched. (3)
There are no virtuous ones who observe the vows of a true person superior to them—those who rescue the wretched who are submerged in the ocean-mire of suffering. (4)
Adopting the highest compassion and remaining unswerving from dharma, the king should wipe away the tears of those who are afflicted and without protectors. (5)
Compassion is considered the supreme duty for all living beings;
therefore, a king should protect the wretched with compassion.
For a king seeking his own happiness should not oppress the wretched;
for a wretched man, when oppressed, destroys the monarch through his wrath.
For who indeed, born into a noble family and enticed by a mere fragment of pleasure, would harm beings of little substance without reflection? (8)
For what person indeed would practice that which is devoid of dharma for the sake of this body, which is beset by mental and physical ailments and destined to perish today or tomorrow? (9)
For that which is led for a moment to a state of endearment by artificial means, one should see this as merely a shadow, like a drop of water. (10)
How indeed can great-souled ones be carried away by the enemies that are the sense-objects, which are as fragile as a mass of clouds tossed about by the blow of a great wind? (11)
The life of embodied beings is indeed as flickering as the moon reflected in water;
knowing it to be such, one should constantly practice what is auspicious. (12)
Perceiving this world to be like a mirage and momentary in its destruction, one should cultivate association with virtuous people for the sake of dharma and happiness. (13)
When attended by virtuous people, a great person shines exceedingly, like a majestic palace smeared with plaster illuminated by the rays of the moon. (14)
Neither the moon-garlanded one nor a lake with blooming lotuses gladdens the hearts as much as the conduct of a virtuous person. (15)
One should abandon association with the wicked, which is as terrifying and shelterless as a parched desert expanse scorched by the rays of the summer sun. (16)
A wicked person, having suddenly entered into one who is endowed with learning and virtue, burns him from within, just as fire consumes a dry tree. (17)
One would rather associate with venomous serpents whose faces are made grey by the smoke of fire vomited from their breath, than with wicked people. 18.
With whichever very same hand the alms-food is given by those with pure hearts, the one of wicked conduct snatches it away from that very hand, just like a cat. (19)
The wicked serpent of an evil person emits a fierce poison of speech that cannot be neutralized even by the best of mantras; he possesses a double-tongued mouth. (20)

Just as a respectful salutation with joined palms is performed for a noble person who is worthy of honor, one who seeks well-being should perform an even more excellent salutation toward a wicked person. (21)
With the desire to truly delight all sentient beings,
one should cultivate supreme loving-kindness and utter worldly speech.
One should constantly gladden people with speech that captivates the mind;
for one who uses harsh speech becomes a source of anxiety, even while being a provider of wealth. (23)
A person who is pierced in the heart as it were and suffers greatly because of such speech—even when oppressed, a wise man should not utter it. (24)
Like weapons, words that are sharp, provocative, and uttered by those lacking self-control cut into the vital organs of embodied beings. (25)
One should always speak only what is pleasant, both to the virtuous and to one's enemies.
To whom is a sweet-spoken person not dear, like a peacock with its sweet cry? (26)
Peacocks are adorned by their cries, which are red with passion; the wise are exceedingly adorned by speech endowed with the quality of sweetness. (27)
The cries of the intoxicated swan, the cuckoo, and the peacock do not captivate the mind as much as the words of a truly wise man. (28)
One who loves virtue, is steadfast, full of faith, and endowed with compassion, should bestow wealth for the sake of dharma while uttering pleasant words. (29)
Those who speak pleasant words and bestow honor, who are illustrious and whose feet are worthy of worship—they are gods in human form. (30)
Pure and with a soul purified by faith, he should always worship the deities;
he should honor his teachers as deities and his friends as himself. (31)
For by prostrating before one's teachers, by emulating the conduct of the virtuous,
and by performing good deeds, one should cause the gods to be well-disposed toward oneself for the sake of prosperity.
One should win over a friend with sincerity, kinsmen with respectful zeal, women and servants with affection and gifts, and other people with courtesy.
Refraining from criticizing the actions of others, fulfilling one’s own duty, compassion toward the wretched, and sweet speech in all circumstances. (34)
Not failing a friend who has come to one's home by withholding even one's life-breaths, embracing him with affection, giving according to one's ability, and practicing forbearance. (35)
Absence of pride in one's own prosperity, lack of envy toward the prosperity of others, speech that does not cause distress to others, and the practice of the vow of silence; ||36||
Maintaining close bonds with kinsmen, acting with integrity toward the virtuous, and conforming to their will—such is the conduct of the great-souled. (37)
For those who abide well in the eternal path,
this is indeed considered the way for householders;
traveling by this path, one certainly attains the state of the great-souled ones.
And he attains this world and the supreme world. ||38||
Thus, when one has set one's self upon the path [of virtue], even an enemy becomes a true friend;
provided it is not out of envy toward the sovereign.
One should bring the world under one's influence through the quality of discipline. ||39||
Where is the pride of a king, and where is the winning over of subjects?
One should attract the world through the application of sweet speech;
for when one is bound by the long tether of sweet words, [the world remains].
For the world does not deviate from its established order even by a single step.
The Fourth Chapter: The Section on the Excellence of the Constituent Elements. The sovereign, the minister, the realm, the fortification, the treasury, the army, and the ally.
This seven-limbed kingdom is said to be mutually supportive. ||1||
Even if deficient by a single factor, this does not function properly; seeking its completeness, one should quickly perform an investigation. (2)
One should first desire for oneself alone to be endowed with virtues; once one is perfected in virtue, one may then proceed to examine others. ||3||
Excellent! The state of being a deity upon earth is difficult to maintain for those who have not disciplined themselves; only one endowed with self-refinement deserves to be a king. (4)
The fortunes of kings, which are the support of the world, are difficult to attain and difficult to maintain;
they remain for a long time within a well-refined self, just as water remains in its receptacle.
Noble lineage, strength of character, age, virtuous conduct, courtesy, promptness in action, reliability, truthfulness, service to elders, and gratitude. ||6||
Endowment with divine fortune, intelligence, a retinue that is not base, having conquerable neighbors, and likewise firm devotion. ||7||
Far-sightedness, enthusiasm, purity, magnanimity, modesty, and righteousness are the qualities that cause a virtuous person to be approached by others. ||8||
Being endowed with these virtues, one is clearly approached [by others];
therefore, one should act in such a way that one becomes approachable by the world. 9.
A king who desires his own welfare should appoint as his retinue those who are of renowned lineage, free from cruelty, pure, and capable of maintaining the world. 10.
Even a wicked king attains the state of being enjoyed [by his subjects] through the virtues of his retinue;
but one with a wicked retinue is like a tree infested by serpents. (11)
Obstructing the path of the virtuous, wicked-minded ministers devour the lord of the earth; therefore, one should be a good minister.
Having attained supreme powers, one should reach a state that is to be enjoyed by the virtuous;
those powers in which the virtuous do not abide are indeed in vain. ||13||
Eloquent, bold, possessed of memory, exalted, powerful, and self-controlled; a skillful leader of the rod of punishment, accomplished in learning, and well-proportioned in body. ||14||

He should be capable of withstanding the attacks of enemies, provide remedies for all perceived threats, observe the vulnerabilities of others, and possess knowledge of the true principles of peace and war. 15.
He should conduct his secret counsel with discretion, knowing the distinctions of place and time;
he should be one who properly acquires wealth and employs it, being a knower of worthy recipients.
Free from anger, greed, fear, malice, arrogance, and fickleness; he transcends the harming of others, calumny, envy, jealousy, and falsehood. ||17||
Endowed with the instructions of the elders, gentle, pleasant in appearance, devoted to virtue, and moderate in speech—this is proclaimed as the excellence of the self. (18)

That king is truly a ruler among men, in whom the people dwell in peace as if with a father—one who is endowed with such virtues as these, who understands the ways of the world, and who is steadfast. (19)
Having obtained a king who is perfectly endowed with the qualities of self-perfection and who acts with propriety, the world prospers like that of Mahendra. (20)
Desire to hear, hearing itself, comprehension, retention, as well as reasoning and critical inquiry, knowledge of the meaning, and knowledge of reality—these are the qualities of the intellect. (21)
Skill, speed, as well as indignation and heroism—characterized by enthusiasm—are the qualities with which one must be endowed to be worthy of being a king. (22)
Generosity, truthfulness, and valor—these three are great virtues;
indeed, a lord of the earth endowed with these attains all virtues. (23)
The ministers of a lord of the earth should be of noble birth, pure, brave, learned, devoted, and practitioners of the science of polity (daṇḍanīti). ||24||

Those who have been thoroughly tested by means of secret trials, who strive properly for the attainment of results, and who are full of devotion, should examine all of his actions—both those performed and those left undone. (25)
Because it is applied by approaching [the object], it is therefore known as *upadhā*;
*upadhā* should be understood as a stratagem (*upāya*), and by means of it, one should examine the ministers. (26)
He is self-controlled, born of a noble lineage, and endowed with family virtue and strength;
he is eloquent, bold, far-sighted, energetic, and possessed of practical resolve. (27)
Free from arrogance and fickleness, friendly, enduring hardships, and pure;
endowed with truthfulness, courage, fortitude, stability, majesty, and health. ||28||
One who has mastered the arts, is skillful, wise, and endowed with retentive memory;
who possesses firm devotion and is free from enmities—such a person should be a minister. (29)
Mindfulness, dedication to the objectives, deliberation, certainty of knowledge, firmness, and secrecy of counsel are proclaimed as the excellence of a minister. (30)
The domestic priest should be proficient in the three Vedas and in the science of government;
he should constantly perform the rites for pacification and prosperity prescribed in the Atharvaveda.
The wise king should examine two qualities in those ministers and those skilled in the sciences: their possession of vision and their proficiency in the arts. (32)
From his own people, he should learn of his family, his status, and his lineage; as well as his skill in various tasks, his specialized knowledge, and his retentive memory. (33)
One should examine the three qualities—eloquence, presence of mind, and likewise [steadfastness];
during the course of conversations, one should discern their skill in speech and their truthfulness.
One should observe his enthusiasm, prowess, as well as endurance of afflictions, fortitude, affection, and steadfastness in times of adversity. (35)

One should learn of another's devotion, friendliness, and purity from their conduct; likewise, one should learn of their strength, character, health, and moral conduct from those who live with them. (36)
One should directly perceive lack of arrogance, steadiness, and the non-committal of hostilities, as well as both nobility and meanness. (37)
In all cases, the activities of qualities that are beyond perception are to be inferred from their actions;
therefore, one should discern the action of those whose activities are imperceptible by means of their fruits. (38)
Ministers should restrain the king when he is intent upon improper deeds;
moreover, the king should listen to the words of even these elders. (39)
When the lord of men closes his eyes, the entire world closes its eyes;
when he awakens, it awakens like a lotus at the rising of the sun. (40)
Therefore, those endowed with intelligence, goodness, and exertion, relying upon Him, should act in such a way that they awaken the Lord of the World so that He may fully realize [the purpose]. (41)
For those who, being unrestrained, restrain him when he has gone astray—those indeed are considered the king's true friends and his true teachers. (42)
Those who restrain a friend from engaging in improper deeds are indeed not friends; they are rather gurus, for they are truly gurus.
Even one who has acquired knowledge is clearly colored by powerful passion;
being one whose mind is stained by passion, what improper act might he not commit? (44)
Even while seeing, a man whose eyes are shrouded by passion remains blind;
friends and physicians treat him with the stainless ointment of discipline. 45.
For a lord of the earth who stumbles, blinded by passion, pride, and intoxication, the actions of a loyal minister serve as a supporting hand. (46)
Indeed, the leaders of a king who is arrogant with pride and follows an unjust course of conduct fall into reproach, like an elephant that is agitated by rut and out of control. //47//
The kingdom prospers through the qualities of the land; that prosperity leads to the king’s own advancement.
Therefore, for the sake of his well-being, a king should dwell upon land endowed with such qualities. (48)
Abounding in crops and mines, endowed with commodities from trade and quarries, beneficial to cattle, rich in water, and filled with meritorious districts. (49)

Land that is delightful, possessing forests of elephants, provided with both water and land routes, and not dependent on rain for its fertility—such land is praised for bringing about prosperity. (50)
The earth became full of gravel and stones, possessed of wildernesses where thieves dwell constantly, parched, filled with thorny forests, and infested with predatory beasts. (51)
The Svājīvya country is endowed with the qualities of earth, possesses marshy lands, and is situated among mountains;
it is populated mostly by Śūdras, artisans, and merchants, and its farmers engage in large-scale enterprises. ||52||
Full of affection, hating his enemies, enduring afflictions, and broad;
crowded with people from various lands, righteous, possessing cattle, and wealthy. (53)
Such a realm is praised, one whose leader is neither foolish nor addicted to vices;
one should strive to increase its prosperity, for from that, everything flourishes. (54)
One should settle in a mountain fortress with wide boundaries and great moats, featuring high walls and gate-towers, and situated near rivers, marshes, and forests. (55)
A great fortress that holds water, grain, and wealth can endure for a long time;
a king devoid of a fortress is like a fragment of a cloud driven by the wind. (56)

Whether it be situated by water, on a mountain, in a forest, in a salt-waste, or in a desert—such a fortress is commended as excellent by those of superior intellect who deliberate upon the construction of fortresses. (57)
The teachers considered a fortress to be preeminent in its security when it is well-stocked with water, food, weapons, and machines, and is occupied by steadfast warriors. (58)
Fortresses with means of retreat, as well as regions consisting of plains and arid lands, are recommended as residences for kings who desire prosperity. (59)
He takes much and gives little; he is renowned and honored by the gods;
he is endowed with all desired objects and is beloved, being presided over by his trusted friends. ||60||

Rich with pearls, gold, and gems, inherited from his father and grandfather, acquired through righteousness, and capable of enduring expenditure—such is the treasury, as approved by those who know state treasuries. (61)
For the sake of dharma, for the sake of wealth, for the maintenance of servants,
and for the sake of misfortune, the treasury must always be protected by one who possesses a treasury.
Inherited from his father and grandfather, loyal, cohesive, paid regular wages, of renowned prowess, born of noble lineage, skilled, and surrounded by capable men. ||63||
Equipped with various weapons, skilled in various modes of combat, surrounded by various warriors, and having had his horses and elephants consecrated with the *nīrājana* rite; ||64||
Exerting effort in the hardships and sufferings of exile and in battles, impartial and consisting primarily of Kṣatriyas—such is the army, according to those who know the science of punishment. (65)
One should make a friend from a noble family—one who is rich in generosity, wisdom, and courage, who has a great following, speaks kindly, is patient for the future, and is free from duplicity. (66)

When hardships arise, even those that are terrible, a friend who is undoubtedly faithful to his father and grandfather, constant, free from duplicity, and dear to the heart— one who can respond to both great and small emergencies— is desired for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose. (68)
Approaching from afar, speech that is clear in meaning and pleasing to the heart, and giving with due respect—this is the threefold way of winning over a friend. (69)
From a friend, one obtains a threefold fruit consisting of the union of Dharma, pleasure, and wealth;
therefore, a wise person should not serve one in whom these three are absent. (70)
At first slender, then broad in the middle, and expanding at every step;
flowing onward and never turning back—such are the friendships of the virtuous, resembling rivers. (71)
A friend born of one's own loins, one bound by affection, one inherited through family lineage, and one protected from calamities—these are to be known as the four kinds of friends. (72)
Purity, generosity, heroism, equanimity in pleasure and pain, affection, skillfulness, and truthfulness are the qualities of a friend. (73)
Devotion to one's purpose and conciseness are the defining characteristics of a friend;
he in whom these are absent is no friend, and one should not place oneself under his protection. (74)
Thus has the entire kingdom been described,
as well as his supreme status, wealth, and means;
all this has been grasped by the skillful minister.
He attains the eternal fulfillment of the three aims of life. ||75||
Just as the inner self, presiding over the primary elements, experiences this entire universe of moving and unmoving beings,
so too does the lord of men, presiding over the constituent elements.
It pervades this entire universe of moving and unmoving beings. ||76||
Endowed with these natural qualities,
he should protect the realm with diligence;
by protecting the realm, he shall endure for a long time.
The king proceeds to the supreme state of glory. ||77||
Endowed with the qualities of his nature, the wise king attains the highest state of desirability;
and he becomes [invincible] in battles against his enemies.
Like a powerful wind amidst the clouds. ||78||
The Fifth Chapter:
On the Conduct of Sovereigns and Subjects.
Those endowed with virtuous conduct [should serve] a king who abides in his duty and is like a wish-fulfilling tree.
Dependents should serve one who is endowed with qualities that attract followers. ||1||
Even one who is destitute of material wealth should be served if he is endowed with the qualities of a worthy master;
for from such a person comes a livelihood that is praiseworthy even after a long period of time.
A wise man should rather sit like a withered stump, wasting away and overcome by hunger, than seek his livelihood from one who lacks self-mastery.
One who lacks self-control and hates right policy, while increasing the prosperity of his enemies, perishes along with that very great sovereignty even after having attained it. (4)
Having gained the opportunity, being skillful, self-possessed, and free from agitation, the minister, firm in his resolve regarding his duties, attains stability in his position. (5)
Whatever may be pleasant to the taste both in the future and in the present, one should perform it even while undergoing hardship; one should not practice what is hated by the world.
Sesame seeds acquire an infused fragrance through contact with campaka flowers;
those who eat garlic take on its odor—all qualities are transmissible. (7)
Even the flow of the Ganges water, upon reaching the ocean, becomes of the same taste as it;
knowing this, one should not resort to that which is of an impure nature.
For even while suffering, the wise person should lead a pure life;
by that, he attains praise in this world and does not fall away from the higher realms. (9)
Seeking success, one should serve a master who is distinguished, steadfast, meritorious, renowned, and frequented by the perfected ones (siddhas),
just as one would serve the praiseworthy Lord of the Vindhyas.
Whatever object one desires in this world, however difficult it may be to attain, the wise person obtains it; therefore, one should exert effort. (11)
A true subordinate, desiring to properly please his sovereign,
should cultivate himself through learning, discipline, arts, and other such qualities.

He possesses noble lineage, learning, scriptural knowledge, magnanimity, artistic skill, valor, and fortitude; he is endowed with a handsome body, courage, strength, health, stability, purity, and compassion. ||13||
One who has transcended backbiting, malice, sowing discord, deceit, greed, and falsehood, and who is free from stubbornness and fickleness, is worthy to perform service. 14.
Skillfulness, goodness, steadfastness, patience, endurance of afflictions, contentment, moral conduct, and energy adorn a subordinate. (15)
Constantly devoted to purity of purpose and endowed with these qualities, one who is already prosperous should inspire confidence in the king for the sake of his own welfare. (16)
Having entered and standing properly in the appropriate place, well-attired and endowed with humility, one should wait upon the king at the proper time.
One should abandon sitting on a seat higher than that of another, cruelty, arrogance, and envy;
one should also not engage in contentious speech with a superior. (18)
One should avoid deception, illusion, hypocrisy, and theft;
and one should pay homage to one's sons and to the favorites of the king. (19)
One should not say anything unpleasant even to one's companions in jest;
for they strike at one's vital points through laughter itself in the assembly. (20)
Standing at his master’s side, he should not cast his gaze elsewhere;
he should not say anything to one another, but should remain looking toward his face. (21)
If someone asks, "Who is here?", he should reply, "It is I," and say, "Command me correctly.
He should then carry out that command without delay and to the best of his ability, ensuring it is not performed falsely.
One should avoid speaking loudly, coughing, spitting, as well as contemptuous speech, yawning, stretching the limbs, and cracking the joints. (23)
Having entered with affection into the mind of [the listener], being esteemed as one who understands the mind, and supporting that person's position, he should speak his speech well. (24)
Or, at his command, one may state a matter that has been thoroughly ascertained—whether it be the opinion of disputants in assemblies for pleasant conversation or in formal debate. (25)
Even though he understands, he should not utter a retort to his master;
for even a learned and intelligent man should avoid arrogance.
Even if one knows [someone] to be superior, one should speak of them with humility;
endowed with modesty, one should describe their excellence through their actions. || 27 ||
In times of calamity, when one has gone astray, or when the time for action has passed—
even if unasked— one who seeks the welfare of others should speak words that are auspicious.
One should speak what is pleasant, true, and beneficial, and that which pertains solely to dharma and artha;
one should avoid that which is untrustworthy, vulgar, behind someone's back, or harsh. (29)
Knowing the proper place and time, one should accomplish the welfare of others at the right place and time;
and being skilled in one's own interest, one should accomplish one's own welfare through a skillful agent who acts for that purpose.
One should not disclose the secret rites or the mantra to one's husband;
nor should one even mentally contemplate hostility or destruction [toward him]. (31)
One should avoid association and gathering with women who behold him, with evildoers, and with messengers of enemies; one should avoid such company that shares a common purpose. (32)
One should not imitate the dress or speech of the lord of the earth;
for even a wise man, though accomplished, does not compete with his qualities.

One who knows the true nature of gestures and appearances, and understands signs through both gestures and appearances, should discern the master’s affection or lack thereof by performing virtuous deeds. (34)
Upon seeing him, he becomes pleased and receives his words with respect;
he offers a seat nearby and inquires after his welfare. (35)
He feels no hesitation in secluded places where the truth can be seen, nor in secret; he listens intently to conversations concerning that goal and those who have realized it. (36)
He praises those worthy of praise, and when being praised himself, he rejoices;
during intervals of conversation, he remembers them with joy and proclaims their virtues. (37)
When spoken to with wholesome advice, he endures it; he does not tolerate censure;
he carries out what has been told to him, and he holds that speech in high esteem. ||38||
He is pleased when there is prosperity, he feels distressed in times of misfortune, and he displays indifference toward both benefits and extraordinary wonders. (39)
He declares that an action performed by one person was performed by another;
he foments opposition and even overlooks destruction. ||40||
That speech which increases hope regarding a task but makes its result otherwise than expected—
even if it is somewhat sweet— is harsh in its underlying meaning.
He engages solely in self-praise and the disparagement of others;
though free from anger, he appears angry, and though serene, his state is fruitless. (42)
He laughs suddenly, walks away, and looks with harshness; when asked for advice regarding his livelihood, he rises abruptly and departs. (43)
He strikes [others] while uttering mantras, falls into laughter, treats faults with indifference, and brings about the destruction of one's livelihood. ||44||
Even when his words are well-spoken, he supports them otherwise;
becoming insipid, he interrupts the discourse at an improper time. (45)
Though being attended upon while lying on his bed, he remains as if asleep;
even when propitiated with great effort, he behaves as though he were slumbering. (46)
These and other such signs characterize one who is attached and one who is detached. One should seek service from the attached person and abandon the detached one. ||47||
One should not abandon even a husband devoid of virtues in times of distress;
for there is no one superior to him who stands by one in calamities. (48)
Those rich in courage do not come to notice when things are proceeding normally;
it is only during the conflict of those who bear the burden of action that their names truly excel.
The helpfulness of the great is indeed praiseworthy and gladdening;
even when slight, it brings about great prosperity by bestowing welfare at the proper time. (50)
In brief, the restraint from what ought not to be done and the adherence to what ought to be done constitute the virtuous conduct of kinsmen, friends, and dependents. (51)
Attendants moving about the king during drinking bouts, women's quarters, and gambling circles should awaken him from his negligence by means of devices such as water-clocks and the like. (52)
For those who neglect a king who is attached to improper acts, being themselves undisciplined in soul, go to ruin along with him. (53)
"Victory to you! Command us, O Lord! and "May you live long!"—thus, with reverence, servants should perform their service while awaiting his command. (54)
Following the will of one's master is the proper conduct for those who live under another;
for even demons are constantly won over by those who comply with their desires. ||55||
What is difficult for great-souled ones to attain when they are endowed with wisdom, courage, and diligence?
Who in this world is superior to those who follow one's will and speak kindly? (56)
For one who is indolent, easily satisfied, world-weary, and undisciplined, even his mother turns her face away at the time of giving. (57)
The riches of a king are for enjoyment only by those who are brave, those who are wise, and those who are experts in service. (58)
"For even one who is unpleasant may be beneficial," such is the instruction of the elders;
by abiding by the instruction of the elders, one attains the state of being beloved. (59)
A king should be like the rain-cloud, providing the means of subsistence for all living beings;
they abandon one who provides no sustenance, just as birds desert a dried-up lake.
Lineage, conduct, learning, and valor—all of this is not taken into account;
people take delight in a donor, even if he is of bad character and of low birth. (61)
In this world, fortune alone is the true lineage; there is no lineage beyond fortune.
The world follows him in whom both the treasury and the army reside.
People who seek to accomplish their own ends honor those who are standing;
for what man would ever salute again one who has fallen, even as an enemy? (63)
This world of living beings, seeking its own interest, approaches one who is blazing with wealth;
yet when her milk is exhausted and she can no longer provide sustenance, the calf abandons its mother.
Without letting the time pass in vain, the king should provide for his obedient servants a livelihood in accordance with their respective duties.
One must not cause the livelihood to fail at the proper time, in the proper place, or toward a worthy recipient; by the failure of such livelihood, a king becomes censurable.
One should never engage in showering gifts upon unworthy recipients, for that is censured by the virtuous;
what else could result from showering gifts upon the unworthy other than the depletion of the treasury? (67)
Having carefully examined family, learning, sacred knowledge, heroism, good character, past deeds, and the stage of life, a high-minded person should show them respect.
One should not despise those of noble birth who are well-conducted and wise;
for, out of pride, they may abandon their master or even kill him.
One should promote those of middling and low status who are endowed with noble qualities;
as they attain greatness, they cause the lord of men to flourish. (70)
One should not cause those endowed with noble lineage to grow together with the lowly;
for even one who is emaciated, if possessed of discernment, becomes worthy of seeking refuge.
For when this world is without light, the wise do not dwell there;
for in such a place, even a genuine gem is regarded as equal to glass. (72)
Where great-souled ones find rest as if at a wish-fulfilling tree, that person becomes praiseworthy and glorious; for true riches have the enjoyment of the virtuous as their fruit. (73)
What is the use of that prosperity which, though flourishing in this world among the prosperous, is not enjoyed with confidence by kinsmen and friends? (74)
At all points of income, he should appoint trusted and tested officials;
through them, he should collect wealth just as the sun draws up water with its rays.

He should appoint as supervisors over all undertakings those who have practiced their work, who possess knowledge of it, who are pure, who are intent on pure objectives, and who are endowed with diligence.

Whoever recognizes a particular thing should employ it for that purpose, just as the sense organ is employed toward its respective object for the sake of attaining all possible objects without exception. //77//
He should be devoted to the storehouse, for his livelihood depends upon it;
he should neither spend excessively nor waste, but should inspect it every day. (78)
Agriculture, trade routes, fortresses, bridges, the binding of elephants, mining, the extraction of forest products, and the settlement of uninhabited lands. (79)
One should properly cause this eightfold group, established in a healthy state, to prosper;
for the sake of livelihood in this world, one should employ them through their various means of subsistence, provided they are accompanied by the necessary instruments.

By whatever means of livelihood a king, even when impoverished, might increase [his resources], he should not impose any restriction upon those who subsist by trade in each of those respective ways. (81)
Just as one would skillfully protect a crop with thorny branches and use a staff for the sake of its fruit, so too should this world be enjoyed. (82)
The subjects face fivefold fear: from officials, from thieves, from enemies, from those favored by the king, and from the greed of the lord of the earth. (83)
Having set aside these five kinds of fear, the king should take his due share at the proper time for the increase of the three goals of life.
Just as a cow is tended at the proper time and milked, so too are subjects;
and just as a flowering creeper is watered and nourished. (85)
One should cause those who have accumulated [faults] to discharge them, just as one would properly drain malignant ulcers;
and they, being appointed, should conduct themselves toward the king as if toward a fire. (86)
Those wicked ones who do even the slightest injury to the lord of the earth are consumed like moths in a fire, being of deluded mind. (87)
He should thus increase the treasury, supervised by trustworthy experts,
and at the proper time he should effect its expenditure for the attainment of the three aims of life.
For one whose treasury is exhausted for the sake of dharma, even emaciation is beautiful,
like that of the moon in autumn when only the remnants have been drunk by the gods.
"There must be no trust in Bṛhaspati"—this is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
And thus one should be distrustful, while nevertheless remaining engaged in worldly affairs. (90)
One should inspire confidence in those who do not yet trust, but one should not over-trust those who already do;
he in whom one places trust is indeed a worthy vessel for prosperity. (91)
Since thoughts arise moment by moment in accordance with their objects, the yogi should therefore constantly observe them with a concentrated mind, just like a practitioner of yoga. ||92||
For the wise man who does not turn back from exertion and possesses good companions, prosperity follows him constantly like a shadow, ever moving with him;
his dependents are satisfied by his own personal favor.
With sweet speech and a people devoted to his conduct, the king— whose treatises are well-refined and entrusted to most trustworthy hands— remains radiant for a long time. (94)
The Sixth Chapter: On the Purification of Thorns.
One who is skilled in both worldly affairs and the Veda, and who is surrounded by those who are themselves skilled;
The king should attentively consider his kingdom, both its external and internal aspects. ||1||
One's own internal body is declared to be the external kingdom; because of their relationship as mutual supports, these two are considered to be one and the same. ||2||
Since the origin of all the constituent elements of sovereignty arises from the kingdom, the king should therefore cause the kingdom to flourish with every effort. (3)
Seeking to favor the world, he should preserve his body;
for the king, the duty is protection, and the body is the means for accomplishing that duty. (4)
For kings who were like sages engaged in violence that was consistent with dharma;
therefore, one who slays the wicked for the sake of dharma is not tainted by faults. ||5||
Devoted to the protection of the Dharma, the lord of the earth should increase his wealth through righteous means;
he should discipline those subjects who cause harm to others.
That which the noble ones, who know the scriptures, praise while it is being performed is Dharma; that which they censure, they declare to be Adharma. (7)
For a king who understands dharma and adharma, delighting in the teaching of the virtuous, should protect his subjects well and slay those who stand as obstacles. ||8||
Those wicked people who, whether acting alone or in concert, cause harm to the kingdom by being favorites of the king—they are designated as *dūṣyas* (corrupters). //9//
The king should swiftly strike down those who are corruptible by means of secret punishment; or, having publicly disgraced them, he should do so once they have incurred the hatred of the people. 10.
The king should indeed invite a seditious person to a private audience; then, men carrying concealed weapons, having been previously signaled, should enter after him. (11)
For those who have gained access to the inner chambers might search through the trustful [attendants];
being armed, they would clearly say, "We have been employed [for this purpose]. (12)

Having thus corrupted those who are to be corrupted, the king, for the sake of the prosperity of his subjects, should extract the thorn by disciplining them, increasing their fortune and excellence. (13)
Just as a seedling, when subtle, is nourished and protected, comes at the proper time to bear fruit successfully; even so is this progeny. (14)
With a harsh [punishment] one causes agitation; with a mild one, one is held in contempt.
Therefore, without taking sides, one should administer punishment according to what is deserved. 15.
The Seventh Chapter:
The Section on the Protection of the Prince.
For the sake of his own welfare and that of his subjects, the king should provide protection for his son.
Lusting after material objects, they would destroy him if he were not protected. ||1||
Prince-like sons, intoxicated by pride and unrestrained like elephants, kill even their own brothers or fathers when possessed by arrogance. ||2||
Solicited here and there by princes intoxicated with pride, the kingdom is guarded with great difficulty, like a piece of meat sniffed at by tigers. (3)
If, while being guarded, they should somehow find a vulnerability, they will undoubtedly kill their protector, just like lion cubs [kill the one who raised them]. (4)
A king should provide his sons with disciplinary training for their prosperity;
for a family whose princes are undisciplined perishes quickly. (5)
One should consecrate a disciplined, legitimate son as the crown prince;
however, one should place a wicked son under secure restraint, like an elephant that has become unruly.
Even one of very wicked conduct does not deserve to be abandoned by a prince;
for, while suffering, he destroys his father by resorting to another. (7)
For one who is clinging to vice should be tormented by the consequences of that vice;
indeed, one should afflict him in such a way that he may come under the jurisdiction of the ancestors. (8)
The Chapter on Self-Protection:
In regard to vehicles, beds, seats, food, drink, clothing, and ornaments—in all these things—one should avoid anything tainted by poison while remaining ever vigilant. (9)
Having bathed in waters that neutralize poison and adorned with amulets that counteract poison,
he should eat only food that has been tested, accompanied by physicians who are experts in the science of wild animals (*jāṅgala*).
The bhringaraja, the parrot, and the sarika—
these birds cry out intensely, agitated by the sight of the venomous serpent.
The eyes of the cakora bird become devoid of luster from the sight of poison; it is perfectly evident that the krauñca bird intoxicates itself, while the intoxicated kokila dies.
And exhaustion arises for the *jīvañjīva* bird from the mere sight of poison;
one should eat [a substance] that has been tested, even if it is only one of those [poisons]. (13)
Snakes do not exist where peacock feathers have been scattered;
therefore, one should always scatter peacock feathers within the dwelling. 14.
One should first give some of the food to be eaten to the fire for the purpose of examination, and then one should give it to birds; there, one should observe the signs.
Smoke, a flame, and a bluish tint arise from the fire, and a crackling sound is produced;
by food smeared with poison, the death of birds occurs. (16)
Non-cohesion, the presence of water, rapid cooling, discoloration, and likewise excessive oiliness—these are the signs of food smeared with poison. (17)
The condiment quickly becomes dry, and during boiling it turns dark and frothy; furthermore, its smell, touch, and taste perish due to the corruption by poison. (18)
When the taste is vitiated by poison, the shadow may be either excessive or deficient;
moreover, an upward-streaked line and a mass of foam are observed. (19)
The color of milk-spirit (rasa) is blue, that of milk is copper-colored, that of wine and water is like the hue of a cuckoo,
and that of curd tainted by poison is blackish.
And in the middle, there is a line extending upwards. ||20||
In all moist substances contaminated by poison, there occurs an immediate state of wilting,
as well as a state of being overcooked and a bluish-green discoloration from boiling.
And a deep bluish-blackness—thus do those who know it say. ||21||
Due to the application of poison, all that is dry becomes shattered and quickly discolored;
the rough becomes soft, and the soft becomes rough.
And in its vicinity, there is the killing of few living beings. ||22||
There will be a scattering of dark spots on outer garments and bedspreads, and there will be a falling away of threads, fibers, and hairs due to the influence of poison. (23)
And for metals and gems, there is the state of being smeared with dirt and mud, as well as the destruction of their brilliance, luster, weight, color, and touch. (24)
A parched and darkened face, faltering speech, frequent yawning, stumbling, trembling, perspiration, possession, and looking toward the various directions—these are the signs. (25)
There would also be instability in one's own activity and on one's own ground;
one should skillfully observe these signs of those who administer poison. (26)
And having tasted all the medicinal herbs, as well as the drink and water,
with those who prepare them, he should partake of his meals.
Whatever articles for adornment and the like there were, all of them the attendants presented to the lord of men, having been thoroughly inspected and sealed. (28)
Whatever has come from others, all that he should examine; for the king is the protector, and thus he must protect himself from both his own people and from others. (29)
One may mount a vehicle or conveyance that is well-known and provided by those who are trustworthy;
however, one should not travel on a path that is unknown or narrow. (30)

One should appoint as attendants those people whose conduct has been observed to be faultless, who are trustworthy, who have come down through hereditary succession, and who are capable of sharing their resources.
One should keep far away from those who are unrighteous, cruel, those whose faults have been observed, those who have been expelled, and those who have come from others. (32)
One should not board a distressed boat that is tossed by a great wind, lacks a skilled navigator, or is dependent on another vessel. (33)
Beholding his trusted circle of troops stationed upon the riverbank during those scorching days,
he saw that the shoals of fish and the nets of crocodiles had been thoroughly cleared away.
Accompanied by his friends, he should plunge into the water. ||34||
Avoiding the thickets, he approached a pure, outer garden grove,
dwelling there in a manner sweet and befitting his youth.
And one should not become intoxicated by passion for the enjoyment of sense objects. //35//
Mounted on a well-trained and swift carriage, he proceeded along a path easy to travel and suitable for the attainment of his goal,
its inner boundaries well-examined and guarded.
But one with a light digestive system may enter the deer forest. ||36||
One should first have the dwelling purified, even when desiring to enter the mother's presence;
one should enter it following the authoritative scriptures.
And he should not remain in a narrow or dense place. ||37||
When the wind blows, raising clouds of dust, when the time comes with rain-clouds clinging to the falling showers,
or likewise in excessive heat or in darkness.
But being established in his own nature, he would not resort to anything at all. ||38||
In going out and in coming in, he should travel along the royal highway on all sides with his full majesty displayed, having cleared the way of people. (39)
One should not enter places crowded with people during processions, festivals, or assemblies, nor should one rush forward excessively. (40)
Attended by eunuchs wearing robes and turbans,
he should move about within the inner apartments accompanied by hunchbacks, Kirātas, and dwarfs.

The attendants of the inner apartments and the ministers, being pure and skilled in reading the mind, should entertain the lord of the earth with jests, provided they avoid weapons, fire, and poison. (42)
For the royal household troops, well-equipped and esteemed by the virtuous, shall protect the king who has entered the inner apartments, being skilled in his appointed duties. (43)
Men of eighty years and women of fifty would behold the purity of the women of the inner apartments, as well as those who were householders.
Women who subsist on their beauty, having bathed and changed their garments, and being adorned with pure garlands and ornaments, should attend upon the king. (45)

One should never associate with those people within [the monastery] who are deceivers, nor with those with matted hair, nor with those with shaven heads, nor with outsiders, nor likewise with female servants. (46)
Every person within [the city] shall go out and enter only after their movement of goods has been verified and they have been identified by the officials.
A lord of the earth should not look upon a dependent who is unwell, except in the case of a life-threatening illness;
for everyone, the sick man is the superior.

Having bathed, anointed himself, being fragrant, wearing a garland, and adorned with beautiful ornaments, he should look upon the goddess who has likewise bathed, is dressed in pure garments, and is beautifully adorned. (49)
One should not go from one's own residence to the house of a woman;
one should not place trust in women, thinking, "I am extremely dear to her. (50)
Having gone to the queen’s chamber, the brother— her own legitimate son by the King of Kārūṣa— lay hidden within his mother’s bed and killed Bhadrasena.
Having mixed parched grain with poison and enticed him with honey,
the queen struck down the lord of Kāśi while he was alone.
With a poison-smeared gem from Sauvīra on his girdle, he [killed] the king;
with an anklet, Vairūpya; and with a mirror, Jāruṣya. (53)
Having placed a weapon in his braid of hair, as well as upon Viḍūratha,
he should avoid the conduct of a serpent and employ both types of enemies.
He whose wife is well-guarded by trustworthy men has both worlds held in his hand, endowed with all enjoyments. (55)
Desiring righteousness, the lord of men, strengthened by aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*), should daily and constantly approach all his wives in due order. (56)
Having deliberated upon the components of his duties at the close of day,
and having dismissed the world [of affairs], he— his actions performed with delight by his wife— [should act] indeed with a hand that is virtuous and bound without weapons.
He should sleep without attachment, protected by those most worthy of trust. ||57||
When the lord of men remains awake incessantly according to the right method,
his subjects sleep here happily and free from anxiety; but when he sleeps with a heedless mind, they sleep in fear of trembling.
By his wakefulness, this world is oppressed. ||58||
Thus did the ancient sages speak regarding the virtuous protection of both the king and the kingdom;
therefore, protecting these very principles in such a manner through wise policy—
The lord of men should proceed toward being skillful in protection. ||59||
The Eighth Chapter:
The Section on the Source of the Circle of States.
Accompanied by the treasury and the army, together with his ministers and counselors—
Stationed in a fortress, the lord of the mandala should contemplate the virtuous circle. ||1||
Like the moon with its unbroken orb, he is pleasing to all beings;
therefore, one who desires victory should always maintain a full circle [of allies]. (2)
Like a charioteer, the king shines as he moves within a pure realm;
in an impure realm, everything falls apart like the wheel of a chariot. //3//

Ministers, the kingdom, fortresses, the treasury, and the army as the fifth—these are declared by those who know [statecraft] to be the constituent elements (prakṛtis) of one who desires victory. ||4||
"These five, as well as the friend and the lord of the earth as the seventh—thus did Bṛhaspati declare that the kingdom consists of seven constituent elements. (5)

But one who is endowed with [the six] constituent elements, possesses great energy, has exerted effort, and is habitually inclined toward conquest, is known as a *vijigīṣu* (one desiring victory). ||6||
Noble lineage, service to the elders, enthusiasm, generosity, knowledge of the mind, intelligence, eloquence, and truthfulness; ||7||
Lack of haste, lack of meanness, humility, self-reliance, knowledge of place and time, firmness, and endurance of all afflictions. ||8||
All-knowingness, skillfulness, vigor, mastery of counsel, reliability, heroism, knowledge of devotion, and gratitude; ||9||
Affection for those who have come for refuge, impatience with injustice, lack of fickleness, having seen the scriptures regarding one's own duties, skillfulness, and far-sightedness. ||10||
Endurance of fatigue, eloquence, having a non-cruel retinue, and natural expansiveness—these constitute the emergence of qualities for one who desires victory. (11)
Even if he is devoid of all other virtues, that king is truly powerful who possesses majesty;
others tremble before one endowed with majesty, just as deer do before lions. (12)
A king endowed with majesty attains great prosperity;
therefore, a lord should generate majesty through the application of exertion. 13.
Adherence to the same objective is said to be the characteristic of an enemy; however, a formidable foe is remembered as one who possesses the qualities of a conqueror. (14)
Avaricious, cruel, lazy, untruthful, negligent, timid, unstable, foolish, and one who disregards his warriors—such an enemy is said to be easily destroyed. ||15||

The enemy, the friend of the enemy, the friend of the friend, and beyond that the friend of the enemy’s friend—likewise the friend of the enemy’s friend and the neutral (udāsīna)—these stand before the one who desires victory. (16)
Beyond that is the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*), after him the rear-enemy (*ākranda*), and then the two types of allies (*āsāra*); these are situated behind the seeker of victory (*vijigīṣu*). (17)
The middle king is the one situated between the enemy and the conqueror, bordering their territories;
he is capable of supporting them when they are united and of subduing them when they are divided. (18)
Outside the circle, there is one who is indifferent yet possesses superior strength;
he is capable of favoring those who are united and of slaying them when they are divided. (19)
These four are proclaimed as the root natures;
thus the one skilled in mantra has declared the mandala to consist of a tetrad. (20)
The seeker of victory, the enemy, the friend, the rear-attacker, the middle king, the neutral king, and the two lords of Puloma—these they declared to be the sixfold circle [of kings]. (21)
The neutral king, the intermediate king, and the circle of kings surrounding the seeker of victory—Uśanas declared this circle of twelve kings. (22)
Regarding the twelve types of kings, the great seers have stated that their enemies and friends are each divided into six groups, making thirty-six in total.
In this world, men declare that for each of the twelve kings, there are five distinct constituent elements (prakṛtis),
beginning with the ministers.
These twelve primary [elements], as well as those beginning with the ministers, constitute the circle of all constituent elements, numbering seventy-two. (25)

The ally associated with both enemy and friend, as well as the enemy-ally and the friend-ally, along with the twelve hereditary kings—these constitute the eighteen-fold circle, according to the Teacher. (26)
Of these eighteen [categories], the ministers and so forth are each distinct;
indeed, the wise know this mandala to consist of one hundred and eight [deities]. ||27||
These eighteen, along with their respective enemies and friends, amount to fifty-four; thus Viśālākṣa declares. (28)
The ministers and other attendants of each of the fifty-four kings, together with twenty-four [deities], constitute this mandala of three hundred. (29)
That which consists of seven constituent elements for both the seeker of victory and the enemy is declared here to be the fourteenfold circle [of states]. (30)
They say that the circle consists of three: the conqueror, the enemy, and the intermediate state;
others have declared it to be six, when these are each joined with their respective allies. (31)
The subjects, beginning with the ministers, belong to each individual king;
those who know the mandala describe the circle as consisting of thirty-six [elements]. (32)
All those seeking victory—the conqueror, the enemy, and the intermediate state—are of seven constituent types;
thus say others who are proponents of political science, making twenty-one in total. (33)
The four hereditary kings together with their respective allies make eight; these, along with the ministers and others, are said in this world to be equal in number to the letters [of the alphabet].
Furthermore, those who are proclaimed as being ahead of and behind the seeker of victory [are likewise included].
Those who know the mandala declare this to be the tenfold mandala. || 35 ||
Those who know the mandala declare that the circle of ten regional rulers, along with their respective ministers and others, consists of sixty members.
The two [kings] to the east and the two to the west, together with the one who desires victory, constitute a group of five;
and when their respective ministers and other attendants are added, they are said to comprise thirty persons. (37)
"Even for others it is exactly thus," so it has been seen by the best among those who possess vision;
the wise have determined that both the pentad and the triad are logical as mandalas. (38)
Parāśara stated that only two fundamental types are logical:
the plaintiff, who is the primary party, and likewise the other, who is the defendant. (39)
Because the enemy and the seeker of victory mutually desire to overcome one another, their states as "enemy" and "seeker of victory" are thus essentially a single constituent element. (40)
Thus they describe the mandala in many ways;
indeed, the clearly manifest one consisting of twelve kings is well-known throughout all the worlds. (41)
He who knows the tree that has eight branches, four roots, sixty leaves, and stands upon two [bases]; that has six flowers and three fruits—he is a knower of policy.
The section on the purification of the mandala:

The rear-attacker (pārṣṇigrāha) and his supporter (tadāsāra) are proclaimed as the enemy and the friend; then the ally (ākranda) and his supporter are likewise declared to belong to the one who desires victory (vijigīṣu). (43)
One should march forward, having first secured both friends as rear-guards; and one should treat the enemy and that friend as if they were two rear-guards in relation to the two front positions. (44)
But having first secured both the friend of the enemy's friend and the mutual friend by means of one who has already accomplished his purpose, the lord of men should then advance. (45)
One should afflict the rear-ward ally (pārṣṇigrāha) by means of one's own ally (ākranda),
and likewise afflict the core support (āsāra) of that rear-ward ally by means of an ally who is itself supported by that same core.
One should effect the uprooting of the enemy by means of both an ally and oneself;
for, through an ally who has allies in turn, one should afflict the enemy's ally. (47)
The lord of the earth should indeed cause affliction to the enemy's friend by means of both the neutral friend and the friend of the friend. (48)
By this sequential method, the seeker of victory, ever alert,
should afflict the harmful enemy from time to time through his allies.
For when an enemy is oppressed on both sides by wise men who are ever-vigilant, he either meets with destruction or remains under their control. || 50 ||
