By every possible means, one should make common cause with a friend and bring them under one's own influence;
for enemies who have been severed from their friends are indeed easy to destroy. (51)
Friends and enemies alike arise solely because of a cause;
therefore, one should abandon that cause by which enemies are born. 52.
For by means of all [the means of policy] everywhere, primarily, he should win over all his subjects;
through winning them over, the king enjoys prosperity in its entirety. || 53 ||
He should win over those who roam afar, the regional rulers, and others living in fortresses;
for their lives sustain the circle of states in this world. (54)

If the middle king, possessing superior strength, should march out with the desire for conquest, [the conqueror] should remain united with the enemy; if unable [to resist], he should submit through a treaty. (55)

When the one seeking victory [the conqueror] attacks the neutral king, all the rulers of the circle [maṇḍala] should stand together according to the law of the assembly; those who are powerless should submit. || 56 ||
When hardships have arisen, coming together for the sake of accomplishing one's own purpose—to properly cross over such calamities—this is the established principle of the dharma of the Saṅgha. (57)
An enemy is considered to be of two kinds: innate and born of action.
The innate one is one born of one's own family; the other is known as the one born of action. (58)
"Annihilation, diminution, oppression, and likewise emaciation—thus do those who know the science declare the fourfold conduct toward an enemy. (59)
Annihilation (ucchedana) should be understood as the destruction of all primordial nature (prakṛti);
the wise consider the destruction of suitable persons and the like to be diminution (apacaya). || 60 ||
The depletion of the treasury and the army, as well as the execution of high officials—this, the teachers say, is "emaciation" (karśana), which is the ultimate form of oppression (pīḍana). 61.
An enemy situated on the bordering territory can be destroyed even when he is endowed with prosperity, provided he is deprived of his base or has resorted to one who is weak. (62)
At the proper time, one should inflict emaciation and oppression upon one who relies on support;
for they say that a fort or a friend esteemed by the virtuous constitutes such support. (63)
Likewise, Vibhīṣaṇa’s uterine brother and the son of the Sun must be destroyed as one's own enemy, because he has seized all their dominions.
One's own enemy recognizes one's vulnerability, actions, and wealth;
remaining within, he consumes one just as fire burns a dry tree. (65)
One who desires victory, when engaged by a stronger power and situated in a difficult position, should increase the strength of the enemy out of fear for his own destruction. (66)
But when, upon being destroyed, another enemy arises, one should not persist in destroying that [first one]; rather, one should bring him under one's own control. (67)
If an enemy who has entered one's own lineage wavers and is difficult to restrain,
one should swiftly elevate a member of that same family to bring him under control.
Poison is countered by poison; a thunderbolt is shattered by a thunderbolt;
and a lordly elephant is slain only by a lordly elephant who has perceived its true strength.
A fish undoubtedly preys upon another fish, and a kinsman upon a kinsman;
yet for the sake of destroying Rāvaṇa, Rāma honored Vibhīṣaṇa.
A wise person should not perform that action which causes the agitation of the circle; rather, one should seek to please the subjects.
One should win over one's own subjects through conciliation, gifts, and honor; however, one should alienate those belonging to others by means of sowing dissension and punishment. 72.
The entire circle is crowded with both friends and enemies;
every person in the world is intent on their own self-interest—how, then, could there be any neutrality anywhere? (73)
One who, having attained wealth, acts with such corruption that he oppresses even a friend,
and who destroys one who has become utterly perverted— he is considered a more wicked enemy.
If a friend who possesses a dual nature acts with partiality, one should swiftly destroy him, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt destroyed Triśiras. (75)
One should even make enemies into friends who bring about prosperity;
yet one should abandon even those who are friends if they persist in doing harm.
He is a kinsman who binds one with great concern for one's welfare;
he is a friend who is both affectionate and dispassionate, and who renders assistance. (77)
Having examined a friend repeatedly, one should abandon him once his faults are known;
for by abandoning one who has no faults, he indeed destroys both dharma and artha.
One should personally investigate faults and virtues everywhere and at all times;
once the faults have been personally identified, the infliction of punishment is commendable. (79)
For one should never become angry without first knowing the fault in its true nature;
people regard one who is angry without cause as being like a venomous snake. (80)
One should discern the differences among friends—those who are equal, superior, or inferior—and likewise distinguish between tasks that are of medium, great, or small importance. (81)
For one should neither bring false accusations nor listen to such things;
one should abandon all those who would cause a breach of friendship. 82.
One should recognize speech that is preparatory, envious, indifferent, or partial, as well as speech accompanied by an illustration and likewise speech accompanied by regret. (83)
One should not oneself take the side of those who are openly hostile toward friends;
rather, one should personally and swiftly prevent mutual resentment among them. (84)
For because the task at hand is of great importance, one who knows the proper time should conceal even the actual faults of subordinates and speak of virtues, even those that are non-existent. (85)
A king should generally make friends who remain so in all circumstances;
for one with many friends is able to bring his enemies under control. (86)
Neither a brother, nor a father, nor any other person remains there [in the afterlife];
for men, it is only a true friend who stands by them when misfortune strikes. (87)
One should subdue enemies from all sides by means of allies firm in their vows;
thus do those who know the circle describe the conduct of the circle (maṇḍala). 88.
The circle [of states] consists of nothing more than allies, neutrals, and enemies; the thorough accomplishment regarding these is known as the purification of the circle. (89)
Thus, proceeding by the path of policy, the king,
being industrious, should practice the purification of his circle;
he shines brilliantly when his circle is thoroughly purified.
Like the autumnal moon, he delighted the subjects. || 90 ||
The Ninth Chapter:
The Section on the Alternatives of Peace.
When a king is attacked by one who is stronger and has no other remedy, [he should resort to peace].
Having fallen into calamity, one should seek peace while biding one's time.
The skull, the offering, the lineage, the association, the proposal, the remedy, the union, and the other person. (2)
The unseen man, the commissioned one, the seizure of one's own flesh, the purchase, the severed one, and likewise the defiler of others. (3)
The junction (sandhi) brought about by the *skandha* is proclaimed as the sixteenth;
thus, those expert in junctions declare the junction to consist of sixteen [parts]. 4.
The joint of the skull (kapāla-sandhi) should be known as consisting solely of a level junction;
that which arises from the act of giving is called the offering (upahāra). || 5 ||
The connection of continuity is to be understood as being preceded by the giving of a daughter;
however, the connection through association with the virtuous is declared to be preceded by loving-kindness.
But he who, for as long as the span of life lasts, shares the same purpose and objective, and who is not divided by any causes in times of prosperity or adversity; (7)
In this context, *saṅgata* is indeed a *sandhi* (junction) because of its excellence, like gold;
it is described as "golden" (*kāñcana*) by others who are skilled in *sandhi*. (8)
That which is performed with a view toward the successful accomplishment of a single purpose is called an "upanyāsa" by those skilled in such applications.
"I have previously rendered assistance to him; he will repay me"—a treaty made with this thought is called *pratīkāra* (reciprocity). || 10 ||
I shall do him a favor, and he will do one for me;
this is a reciprocal service, like that between Rāma and Sugrīva.
When two parties go on an expedition having correctly directed their efforts toward a single objective,
that joint advance is called the "alliance of conjunction" (saṃyoga-sandhi).
"Let our two chief warriors accomplish my purpose"—when such a wager is made, that is a peace treaty mediated by another person. (13)
"By you alone this purpose of mine must be accomplished"—where an enemy makes such a wager, that is known as the *adṛṣṭapuruṣa* (the "unseen man"). || 14 ||

When a powerful enemy is made to enter into a treaty by those skilled in diplomacy on the condition of surrendering only a portion of his territory as a price, that is declared to be [the type of peace] called *ādiṣṭa*. (15)
An alliance with one's own army is known as "offering oneself as bait";
it is undertaken for the sake of preserving one's life, wherein all else is surrendered as a means of securing support. (16)

Whether by means of a portion of the treasury, or base metals, or even the entire treasury, the purchase of peace (parikraya) is declared for the purpose of protecting the remaining constituents of the state. ||17||
By the gift of lands that are rich in essence, one is said to be "Ucchinna";
by the gift of the fruits arising from all lands, one is "Paradūṣaṇa. (18)
Where a limited result is led from one aggregate to another aggregate, those who know the joints call that a *sandhi* (joint) which is to be conveyed by the aggregates. || 19 ||
Mutual assistance, friendship, kinship, and tribute—these four others are to be known as types of alliance. (20)
Indeed, it is our view that there is only one type of peace treaty, namely the *upahāra*;
for all other varieties, excluding the *maitra*, are merely different forms of the *upahāra*. (21)
Since an aggressor who possesses superior force does not desist without having achieved his goal, no other form of peace exists for him except through the payment of tribute. (22)
A child, an old man, one afflicted by a chronic disease, as well as one excluded from his kin;
a coward, one whose people are cowardly, a greedy man, and likewise one whose people are greedy. (23)
One whose nature is dispassionate yet who is excessively attached to sense objects, one whose counsel is divided by a distracted mind, and one who reviles the gods and the Brahmins. || 24 ||
Struck by fate, as well as one who merely contemplates fate;
afflicted by the calamity of famine, and beset by the misfortunes of his army. || 25 ||
One who stays in an improper place, one with many enemies, one who is bound by time,
and one who is devoid of truth and dharma— these twenty are the types of men.
One should not make peace with these, but should instead wage war against them alone;
for when they are attacked, they certainly fall under the power of the enemy. (27)
For because a fool lacks power, the world does not wish to fight for him;
indeed, who would fight on behalf of another when he himself is unable to fight? (28)
Because they lack the power of enthusiasm, both an old man and one afflicted by a chronic illness are undoubtedly despised even by their own kin. (29)
For one who is excluded from all kinsmen becomes easy to destroy;
yet those very kinsmen, once he has brought them under his own control, will slay him.
A coward perishes quickly by abandoning battle;
even a hero is abandoned by those [companions] in combat if he acts like a non-hero. 31.
Because of his greed and lack of generosity, his dependents will not fight for him;
a king who depends on greedy men is slain by those very same men once they have been won over by gifts.
One whose constituents have become disaffected is abandoned by those very constituents in battle;
whereas one who is excessively attached to sense objects finds his application of effort directed toward pleasure.
One whose mind is manifold regarding mantras becomes detestable to practitioners;
because his mind is unstable, he is neglected by them in the performance of rites.
Because the power of Dharma is ever supreme, one who reviles the gods and Brahmins is himself utterly destroyed,
being likewise struck down by fate.
"In prosperity as well as in adversity, fate alone is the cause";
thinking thus and devoted to fate, one does not exert oneself by one's own effort. (36)
One who suffers from the calamity of famine perishes by his own accord;
and for one beset by the calamity of his forces, there is no power to fight. (37)
For one who stays in an improper place is slain even by a very small enemy;
even a tiny crocodile drags down a lordly elephant in the water. (38)
But one who has many enemies is terrified like a pigeon in the midst of hawks;
by whichever path he goes, by that very path he quickly perishes. 39.
An army engaged at an improper time is destroyed by one who fights at the right time, just as a crow is killed by an owl when its vision is lost in the dead of night. 40.
One should never, under any circumstances, form an alliance with one who has departed from truth and righteousness;
for even if such a person is allied, they will soon undergo a change of character due to their inherent wickedness.

One who is truthful, noble, righteous, and noble, one who has a united brotherhood, one who is powerful, and one who is victorious in many battles—these seven are proclaimed as those with whom one should form an alliance. || 42 ||
Guarding his truth, the noble man does not undergo change even when committed to truth; even in the face of threats to his life, he clearly never descends to ignobility.
For when a righteous man is attacked, everyone indeed fights for him;
because of the subjects' affection and his righteousness, a righteous man is difficult to overcome even through hardship. (44)
Indeed, one should form an alliance even with a base person, for once gained, he may destroy him;
like the son of Reṇukā, he does not remain even at his roots.
Just as a bamboo thicket, dense and surrounded by thorns,
cannot be uprooted, so too one who possesses a multitude of brothers cannot be destroyed.
For one who has been overpowered by a stronger being, even though he exerts every effort, there is truly no refuge at all, like that of a deer overcome by a lion. (47)
Even when exerting himself only slightly, a powerful lion slays even rutting elephants; therefore, one who desires his own welfare should make peace with him.
There is no precedent for one to fight with a stronger opponent;
indeed, a cloud never moves against the wind.
For those who bow before the powerful and even advance against them at the right time,
their fortunes do not depart, just as rivers flow toward the lowlands.
Like that of Jamadagni’s son, the prowess of one who has been victorious in many battles is distinguished by its being universal, omnipresent, and eternal. (51)
He who has been victorious in many battles and enters into an alliance—by his majesty, his enemies quickly come under his control. (52)
Even when bound by a treaty, a wise man should never place his trust;
for in ancient times, Indra slew Vṛtra after having made a pact of non-aggression.
Even a son undergoes transformation when he is lapped up by royal power, and the father likewise;
therefore, they say that the conduct of a king is something other than the conduct of ordinary people.
One who is attacked by a powerful foe while stationed in a fortress with diligence should call upon those even more powerful than him for the sake of his own liberation. (55)
"Having observed his own power and energy, he should wage war against one who is greater, just as a lion [assails] an elephant; so says Bharadvāja. (56)
Even a single lion can crush a herd of a thousand elephants;
therefore, viewing oneself as exalted like a lion, one should spring forward.
For one who, possessing a small army, overcomes a superior foe by force and slays him,
all enemies everywhere come under his control through the power of his majesty.
One should desire peace even with an equal, for victory in battle is uncertain;
"one should not engage in what is doubtful," so said Bṛhaspati. (59)
Desiring further growth until it reaches full maturity, one should here seek an alliance with an equal;
or else, as in the case of two unbaked jars, [it would inevitably break].
The equal conjunction [of the humors] is characterized by mutual differentiation. || 60 ||
In battle, destruction is certain for both sides at some point;
were not Sunda and Upasunda, who possessed equal prowess, slain by one another? (61)

For even an enemy who has fallen into misfortune and is deprived of his power should be reconciled when he approaches; for like a drop of water falling upon a wound, he causes pain, just as frost does.
If one is inferior, one should not desire a treaty; the reason for this is certain.
Having gained his confidence, one should strike him there without any longing [for the alliance]. (63)
Having been outmaneuvered by a stronger opponent, one who is diligent should enter [the enemy's camp] and approach him in such a way that he gains his confidence. 64.
Constantly striving for confidence, with his appearance and actions concealed, he should speak only pleasant words; whatever must be done, that indeed he should accomplish.
Through trust one attains affection; through trust one accomplishes one's purpose.
Indeed, it was through misplaced trust that the Lord of the Gods caused the fall of Diti’s embryo.
Having entered into an alliance with the crown prince or a chief minister,
one who is firm of mind should incite internal rebellion against the attacker.
By means of the relinquishing of great wealth and by means of documents prepared in one's own name, one should effect the subversion of the enemy's resources here in this world. 68.
For when a high minister has been corrupted, even a formidable enemy causes distrust within one's own party; and being in such a state, he becomes inactive. (69)
Having instigated the enemy's ministers, one should bring that undertaking to a halt;
or, by sowing dissension among the physicians, one should cause the enemy to perish through the administration of poison.
One should, with every effort, provoke the enemy's anger later;
then, having pursued that subsequent provocation to its undesirable conclusion, one should attack him. 71.
Through spies residing in that region, as well as through soothsayers,
he should cause the prediction of an impending calamity to be made by means of signs of accomplishment.
Having examined virtuous deeds in light of the defects such as decay, expenditure, exertion, and slaughter,
one may indeed desire even some degree of suffering.
There is no dispute, for the faults arise from that. || 73 ||
Wife, self, friends, and wealth—
all these become useless here in the mere twinkling of an eye; indeed, they are repeatedly thrown into turmoil.
Therefore, a wise person should not be excessively contentious. || 74 ||
For what wise man would place his friends, his wealth, his kingdom, himself, and even his fame upon the swing of uncertainty in battle? (75)
One who is being attacked should seek to bring about peace through conciliation, gifts, and sowing dissension;
desiring peace, one should approach from afar with an even array of troops.
The neighboring king approached, having abandoned all alliance.
Having established his own protection with a well-united force, the wise king, moving against the enemy,
should cause him distress so that he is thoroughly tormented.
When heated, it undergoes union with that which is heated. || 77 ||
Thus indeed did the ancient great seers, the most skilled in treaties, declare regarding peace;
therefore, O Lord of Men, let the king act accordingly with discipline.
Having examined the task, whether it be major or otherwise, [one should act] in two ways.
The Tenth Chapter:
The Section on the Alternatives of War.
For those seized by indignation, whose minds are tormented by wrath:
Through mutual injury, conflict arises among men. || 1 ||
One who desires his own prosperity, or one who is being oppressed by another, should indeed initiate hostilities if he is endowed with the advantages of place, time, and strength. (2)
The seizure of kingdom, women, status, and country, as well as of knowledge and strength; intoxication, pride, and likewise affliction arising from sense objects. || 3 ||
The impairment of knowledge, wealth, power, and virtue, as well as destiny itself, the humiliation of one's friends, and likewise the destruction of kinsmen—[all these arise from anger]. (4)
The cessation of favor toward living beings, the defilement of the mandala, and the obsession with a single purpose—these are the sources of conflict. || 5 ||
By the gift or the restraint of the kingdom, women, estates, and territories, the pacification of war is prescribed by those who know the proper means. (6)
This very same [remedy] should be understood as applicable when [the enemy's] own purpose or dharma is obstructed;
however, when [the enemy's] objects are destroyed, the remedy is the crushing of the enemy's objects. (7)
When [anger] arises from the theft of knowledge or from the obstruction of the power of knowledge,
its pacification occurs through the renunciation of that object, or through patience, or through indifference.
One should remain indifferent even toward a circle of friends if they are joined with unrighteousness and malice;
however, for the sake of a friend who possesses self-control, one should even sacrifice one's own life.
One should bring to pacification with honor that [anger] which has arisen from an insult; however, for anger born of pride, the means should be conciliation first, or else a prostration.
Through secret application or by means of secret rites,
the wise man should pacify the conflict arising from the destruction of kinsmen.
A wise person should make such a renunciation of wealth that no suffering arises, when that wealth is produced through attachment to a single object. 12.
One should never engage in conflict arising from the seizure of wealth;
for in some instances, such a quarrel among men may even lead to total ruin. (13)

One should bring about the pacification of a dispute arisen among a great multitude by means of presenting what has been witnessed, as well as through gifts and the like, and by means of sowing dissension.

The self-controlled one should bring to an end that which arises from the interruption of favor toward living beings; however, when a calamity arises from fate, pacification through fate alone is approved by the wise. 15.

One should bring to pacification, through skillful means, the agitation of the circle that has arisen—whether it be caused by a rival wife, by the site of the house, by a woman, by speech, or by an offense. (16)
Enmity is traditionally said to be of five kinds by those skilled in the classification of enmity:
that which arises from the obstruction of land, and likewise that which is born from the impairment of power.
The son of Bāhudanti declared that enmity is of four kinds: that arising from the succession of lands, as well as that born from the disturbance of a mandala. (18)
Men say that there are exactly two kinds of enmity arising from the offenses of one's family:
that which yields some fruit, that which is fruitless, and that which has uncertain fruit. (19)
That which produces a fault in the present and is also fruitless in the future;
likewise, that which produces a fault both in the future and in the present. (20)
Or even if he is exhorted by others who lack full understanding of his vigor—for the sake of another's welfare and on account of a woman—for a long time by the best of the twice-born; (21)
At an improper time, by one joined with fate and accompanied by strength extracted through force,
it may yield fruit in the present moment but be devoid of fruit for the future.
One should never engage in this sixteenfold dispute, which yields fruit in the future but is likewise fruitless in the present.
A wise person should undertake that which is pure both for the present and the future;
they should contemplate all actions that are pure for both the present and the future. (24)
One who abides in that which is pure in both the present and the future incurs no reproach;
a wise man should perform actions that are beneficial for both worlds, and he should not abandon this world out of greed for even a fragment of wealth. (25)
One should abandon from afar one who performs actions contrary to the next world;
because this is the authority of the scriptures, one should practice what is wholesome and auspicious. (26)
When the wise man perceives his own force to be joyful and well-nourished, while that of the enemy is the opposite, then he should wage war. (27)
When one's own circle of subjects is prosperous and loyal, while that of the enemy is the opposite, then one should wage war. (28)
When it is clearly observed that fate has turned against one's enemy, then one should engage in conflict. (29)
When one's allies, vanguard, and reinforcements are firmly devoted, while those of the enemy are the opposite, then one should wage war. (30)
Land, a friend, and gold—these three are the fruits of war; when these are certain to be obtained, then one should engage in war. (31)

The teacher’s wealth is more important than that; the friend is more important than that; the land is more important than that; all prosperities arise from the land, and from them come the circles of kinsmen and friends.
A wise man should employ strategic means against an enemy who is equal in all resources;
when the enemy is equal and cannot be countered by such means, the use of force is praised.
A wise man, perceiving that war has arrived, should bring it to peace through strategic means;
for since victory is uncertain, he should not rush headlong into it.
Overpowered by one who is stronger while desiring unshakable prosperity, one should always adopt the conduct of a reed and never that of a serpent. (35)
By acting gradually like a reed, one attains great prosperity;
but by acting like a serpent, one meets only with death.
Remaining like one intoxicated or heedless, the wise man should spring forward and swallow his prey—
provided it is not likely to escape and has come to him in due course— just like the king of beasts.
Adopting the contraction of a tortoise, one should endure even a blow;
but when the right time has come, the wise man should rise up like a fierce serpent. (38)
At the proper time, one should be as enduring as a mountain, yet at the right moment, as impatient as fire; one may even carry [the enemy] on one's shoulder while uttering pleasant words,
but when the time arrives, one should shatter him like a jar against a stone.
People are always intent on their own interests; therefore, one should apply the remedies as prescribed so that one’s own purpose may be accomplished. 40.
Having entered the enemy's heart without interval through the conduct of favor and the conduct of the world,
he indeed remained there, holding the time by the hand of policy.
One should forcibly seize Fortune by her hair. || 41 ||
One born of noble lineage, possessing perfect and noble prowess,
steadfast, grateful, wise, and powerful;
one who is exceedingly generous and affectionate toward those who approach him.
They say that an enemy is exceedingly difficult to appease. || 42 ||
Untruthfulness, cruelty, ingratitude, fear, negligence, laziness, despondency,
as well as vain pride and procrastination.
Likewise, [the destruction of] women, dice, and so forth, leads to the ruin of prosperity. || 43 ||
Thus, one endowed with the three powers should swiftly advance against a hateful enemy possessed of faults, desiring victory;
otherwise, he is esteemed by virtuous people.
The ignorant person brings about injury to himself. || 44 ||
Endowed with the wisdom that seeks to elevate his royal station, and having scrutinized the affairs of the circle of states,
the king has resorted to this path of war.
One with steadfast effort should strive for success. || 45 ||
The Eleventh Chapter: The Section on the Alternatives of Marching, Halting, Double Policy, and Seeking Shelter,
concerning one who possesses superior strength and valor, desires victory, and seeks conquest.
The expedition of one whose subjects are devoted to his virtues is known as "yāna" (marching). || 1 ||
Waging war, making peace, as well as marching in combination, incidental [expedition], and indifference—thus, by the wise, marching is remembered as being of five kinds. (2)
When one proceeds by force against all the enemy's hosts after having declared war, the experts in marching know that as *vigṛhyayāna* (marching after declaring war). || 3 ||
Having by all means and through the strength of one's own allies seized all enemies and friends, the departure for war is known as *vigṛhyagamana* (marching after declaring war). || 4 ||
That journey which is undertaken elsewhere after making peace with a rear-attacking enemy is called "going after making peace"; it is for one who desires victory and seeks results. || 5 ||
When one proceeds together with neighboring kings and confederates who are endowed with power and purity at a single place, that is indeed called *sambhūyagamana* (joint expedition).
But when both sides are enemies, or when two parties are destroying their own respective natures,
it is said that they should travel together, like Hanumān and the Sun.
Having relied upon those of little substance and having promised the arising of results, one proceeds to conquer the enemy; for that indeed is what is called marching together.
Setting out for one place, one indeed goes elsewhere because of attachment; that is called "the vehicle of attachment," and in this regard, the arrow serves as the illustration. (9)
When a powerful king, having marched against an enemy, encounters the manifestation of the fruit [of his action] and disregards the march of an ally, that is called the "neglectful march. (10)
Having bypassed the Nivātakavacas who dwell in Hiraṇyapura,
Dhanañjaya adopted a policy of indifference and slaughtered them.
Women, intoxicants, hunting, dice,
and various forms of gambling—
these are the calamities indeed proclaimed by him.
One who is possessed of [virtues] but is addicted to vices is one who may be approached. ||12||
The "sitting" (āsana) is defined as the non-obstruction of each other's power;
it is said to be fivefold between the enemy and the seeker of victory. (13)
Mutual encroachment is called sitting after having waged war; remaining in one's position after having waged war against the enemy is called sitting after having waged war (vigṛhyāsana). || 14 ||
When an enemy situated in a fortress cannot be captured,
one should sit encamped after having attacked him and cut off his supplies and reinforcements.
When the supply of provisions and reinforcements is cut off, when fodder and fuel are exhausted,
and when the constituent elements of the state become disaffected, one should bring such an enemy under control by means of time alone.
When both the aggressor and the seeker of victory are suffering defeat in war,
their remaining in a state of equilibrium after entering into a treaty is called "staying in wait after making peace" (sandhāyāsana).
Together with the Nivātakavacas, Rāvaṇa, the terror of his enemies,
having placed Brahmā between them, made peace and took his seat.
When both the neutral and the intermediate [powers] remain united due to an equal apprehension of danger, their joint establishment is called *sambhūyāsana* (joint sitting). || 19 ||
For one who desires the destruction of both enemies,
one should join together with him and counter-attack them, being superior in all resources.
When one who desires to go elsewhere sits down due to some incidental circumstance,
that posture is called *prasaṅgāsana* by those who understand its meaning.
Now, indifference toward an exceedingly powerful enemy is called the "posture of equanimity.
Indra maintained equanimity regarding the seizure of the Pārijāta tree.
Or, when one remains seated while being ignored by others for some reason or other, like Rukmin, that is indeed known as the "posture of indifference" (upekṣāsana). || 23 ||
Placing himself between two powerful enemies by means of his speech,
he should conduct himself through a policy of double-dealing, remaining unobserved like the eye of a crow.
Exerting effort, he should manage the one who is closer to those two;
when both have come together, he should serve the stronger of the two. (25)
When both parties, having reached an agreement, do not desire a union,
then one should approach that enemy or seek refuge with another who is superior.
The strategy of sowing dissension is said to be twofold, pertaining to those who are independent and those who are dependent.
That which is independent has been explained; however, the other is one who receives wages from both sides. (27)
When being destroyed by a powerful foe and having no means of resistance, one should take refuge in a noble and truthful person of high lineage who is superior in strength. (28)

Constantly beholding him, worshipping him, being permeated by his nature, acting according to his will, and showing humility—this is remembered as the proper conduct for those who take refuge in him. (29)
Having passed the time there in a disciplined manner, as if with a teacher, one becomes fulfilled through that association and gradually comes under one's own control. (30)
Giving either strength, or treasure, or land, or the produce of the land, one who has no alliance and no support should take refuge with the aggressor. (31)
One who is in distress should give all these for the sake of his own protection;
like Yudhiṣṭhira, he recovers the earth while still alive.
Whether at the attainment of his own self or upon the misfortune of the enemy's fortune, he should strike when powerful, or like a lion, when the opportune time has arisen. (33)
He did not seek association with either a superior or another for no reason,
nor out of fear of the faults arising from loss and expense, or even from the treachery born of misplaced confidence.
Having entered into an alliance with a cause, one should not place trust even in one's father;
for the wicked generally commit treachery against one who has placed trust in them. (35)
Thus, while some declare the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) to be twofold,
it has been proclaimed by the wise that marching (*yāna*) and encamping (*āsana*) are forms of war (*vigraha*),
whereas double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*) and seeking refuge (*samāśraya*) are forms of peace (*saṃdhi*) for those who know the paths of peace. (36)
Since one engages in conflict while approaching and while staying, the wise declare that conflict occurs in both the modes of marching and encamping. (37)
Since there is no duality of support when there is no alliance, therefore both of those are described by the wise as the form of an alliance. (38)
They say that peace and war constitute a "twofold state";
others, however, maintain that these two, along with seeking refuge, constitute a "threefold state. (39)
Because one who is being oppressed by a stronger power might seek refuge with another, Bṛhaspati said that seeking refuge is indeed distinct from making peace. (40)
The state of war (*vigraha*) alone is the primary policy (*guṇa*);
the others, such as peace (*sandhi*) and so forth, are secondary qualities arising from it,
having attained their distinction through different circumstances.
"The sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) alone is the doctrine of our teacher. || 41 ||
The Twelfth Chapter:
The Section on the Deliberation of Counsel.
One whose mind is resolved upon the sixfold policy, who keeps secrets, and who employs secret agents;
One who knows the mantras should deliberate here together with ministers who are likewise knowers of mantras.
A king skilled in the meaning of counsel enjoys happiness and victory;
but one who acts contrary to it is cast aside by the wise, even if he is independent.
Enemies plunder this ill counsel from every side, just as Yātudhānas plunder a ritual intention; therefore, one should be devoted to counsel. || 3 ||
In this world, one should deliberate on affairs of state together with a trustworthy wise man;
however, one should avoid here a fool who appears trustworthy as well as a learned man who is untrustworthy. (4)

One should not abandon the path practiced by the virtuous of old— those who have attained the goal of the true path and perfected their actions— for it is in accordance with the scriptures and leads to success.
One who steps onto a path contrary to the scriptures and rushes headlong into danger does not turn back until he has been swallowed by the edge of his enemy’s sword.
The power of counsel is praised over the powers of majesty and energy;
for Kāvya, though possessed of majesty and energy, was defeated by the priest of the gods.
A lion who has not learned the proper method kills an elephant by force alone;
but a wise and steadfast man may conquer hundreds of them through his intellect.
Beholding from afar the states of woe,
the wise perform actions here for the sake of the fruit alone, having practiced the excellent means.
One should seek [one's goal] preceded by skillful means and spring forth after observing the right time; for one who knows only how to exert valor becomes a cause for regret later.
One should distinguish between what is possible and what is impossible with a clear intellect;
otherwise, it is like striking a mountain with one's tusks merely to break one's own teeth. (11)
For those whose conduct consists of undertaking the impossible, what fruit can there be other than suffering?
For one who attempts to taste the sky, how could there ever be a mouthful of food? 12.
One should not approach fire like a moth; rather, one should touch it only when it is fit to be touched.
For what else could happen to a moth that falls into the fire except for burning? (13)
For one who, out of delusion, exerts effort toward objects that are difficult to attain, the calamities of karma clearly result in intense torment. (14)
With an intellect that has attained awakening, he should investigate the state of perfect excellence, like one with pure steps ascending the lofty peak of a mountain. (15)
The station of kings, which is difficult to ascend and honored by all the world, becomes defiled by even a slight transgression, just as the status of a Brahmin is defiled. 16.
Actions undertaken according to the scriptures by those of pure intellect yield fruit before long, just as enchanting forests do. (17)
For even if an action undertaken with right effort should be fruitless,
it does not cause such torment as that which is pursued through delusion.
But when an undertaking that has been correctly initiated meets with failure, a man should not be blamed therein, for his human effort has been thwarted by destiny. (19)
One whose intellect is unclouded should exert effort for the sake of the fruit;
thereafter, one skilled in the Atharvaveda should rely upon destiny for the remainder. 20.
Having observed both himself and the other, the wise man should rise up;
for this indeed is true knowledge: the realization of both self and other. (21)
A wise person should not perform an action that is fruitless, full of affliction, of doubtful result, or followed by great enmity. (22)
Action that is pure in both the present and the future, inherited through a perfectly pure lineage, and always attended by beneficial consequences, is praised by the virtuous. (23)
One should undertake that action which results in welfare and by which one does not incur blame; for one should apply oneself to such a task even if it is bitter in the immediate present.
An undertaking based on intelligence alone is always superior for the accomplishment of results;
however, in certain cases, the conduct of a lion [through force] is praised as a means of finding a virtuous friend.
It is difficult for the wicked to acquire merit by leaping suddenly at them;
however, by means of a stratagem, one places one's foot upon the head of a rutting elephant.
There is nothing whatsoever here that cannot be accomplished by the wise;
even iron, which is impenetrable, is brought to a state of fluidity through skillful means.
Even a great mass of iron being carried away does not cut; yet that same iron, when made into a blade, accomplishes even the most desired task. (28)
This is indeed well known in the world: water is the restrainer of fire; yet by that very same water, when it is employed with the proper means, the fire may be dried up. (29)
The cognition of what is not yet known, the ascertainment of what has been known, the cutting away of doubt regarding a twofold matter, and the perception of the remainder. (30)
Abiding by the instruction of the wise, one should not despise anyone;
one should listen to everyone with the desire to grasp what is well-spoken. (31)
He who, intoxicated by pride and deluded regarding his duties, transgresses against his minister, will soon find that his enemies bypass him whose counsel is in vain. (32)
One must indeed protect the seed-mantra, for that is the very seed of sovereigns;
when it is broken, division is certain, but when it is guarded, there is unsurpassed security.
When a wise man acts like a lion at the proper time,
his own kin shall perceive his deed as being accomplished by others.
A mantra is considered praiseworthy when it causes no regret, bestows results that follow correctly, does not require a long duration, and is desired. (35)
Companions, the means of accomplishment, the distinction between place and time,
the remedy for misfortune, and success— these are held to be the five constituent parts.
One should carry out what has been commenced and initiate what has not yet begun;
while carrying it out, one should conceal [the process] and bring it to completion with particular excellence. || 37 ||
The knower of mantras should employ [the practice] in various ways through the gateways of activity;
wherever there is equanimity of the mind, by that means one shall quickly ascend.
One should undertake that which one intends to do where there is harmony with the minds of ministers, where the heart feels no apprehension, and where the virtuous do not criticize it. (39)
Even when a counsel has been adopted by those skilled in counsel, one should personally deliberate upon it further;
thus should the counselor act so that he does not harm his own interest. (40)
Out of self-interest, the circle of ministers desires a long-standing state of conflict;
and the king, preoccupied with extensive affairs, becomes their object of enjoyment. (41)
Tranquility of mind, faith, as well as proficiency of the instruments [of action], and the excellence of both assistants and initiative—these are the characteristics of success in undertakings. 42.
Lightness in rising, freedom from obstacles, and the successful accomplishment of one's means—
all these indicate that success in one's undertakings is imminent.
One should repeat the mantra repeatedly and maintain it with great effort;
for a mantra maintained without effort, being unstable, may burn like fire.
Being devoted to it, one should protect the mantra within the lineage of trustworthy recipients;
for a mantra that is not protected indeed causes the succession of trustworthy ones to be broken. 45.
Arrogance, negligence, desire, and the mutterings of sleepers, as well as secret women and those who have been slighted, destroy a secret counsel. (46)
In a place without pillars, without windows, and without shelter from the interior of walls—whether on the roof of a palace or in a forest—one should deliberate in secret, unobserved. (47)
Manu declared that the circle of ministers should consist of twelve, Bṛhaspati said sixteen, and Uśanas said twenty. (48)

Others say "according to what is possible"; having entered there according to the prescribed rule, one with a focused mind should deliberate for the sake of achieving and increasing the success of the task. (49)
Having deliberated again and again on each matter individually, one who seeks his own welfare should enter upon action after considering their opinions one by one. (50)

One who possesses a great following, who has seen the results of his actions according to the scriptures, who is beneficial and wise—whatever such a person, established in the doctrine, may say, that one should perform well. (51)
One should not let the time for action pass after having made a determination regarding the mantra; however, if that time has elapsed, one should arrange it again as is appropriate.
A wise person should never let the time for action pass by;
for the conjunction of circumstances necessary for action occurs only rarely and is very difficult to attain. (53)
A wise person should perform action at the proper time by following the path of the virtuous;
performing it at the right time, he enjoys a fruitful result that is full of essence. 54.
Observing both this and that, being well-supported by time, place, and allies,
and having secured his rear, he should advance against a worthy object and not out of impetuosity.
A person of small intellect, regarding what is harmful as beneficial, might disregard the counsel of his ministers;
being fickle, he may rush forward with impetuosity.
Struck by an enemy’s sword, he awakens. || 56 ||
Without considering the relative strength and weakness of his enemies,
he was arrogant, thinking "it is I," and being fickle, he rushed forward according to his own whim.
One who is not humble and whose mind is small does not understand. || 57 ||
Thus, by the power of the mantra, the lord of the earth,
established upon the path of policy through discipline, [subdued] those who were like great, wicked serpents.
Endowed with diligence, he brings his enemies under his control. || 58 ||
The Thirteenth Chapter: The Section on the Dispatch of Messengers.
Having deliberated and being well-versed in counsel, he [the king] acted according to the consensus reached by his ministers.
One should dispatch a messenger, who considers himself a messenger, to the one against whom one intends to march.
Bold, possessed of a retentive memory, eloquent, well-versed in both weaponry and sacred scriptures, and trained in the duties [of his office], such a person is fit to be the king's envoy. (2)

The envoy is traditionally held to be of three kinds: one with full discretionary powers, one with limited authority, and likewise one who merely carries a command; by implication, he may also be deficient in capability. ||3||
He should go forth by his master’s command, for he must proceed further and further, reflecting on his own words and the words of others, both what has been said and what is yet to be said. (4)
He should appoint frontier guards as well as forest-dwelling allies;
he should also know the water reservoirs and the roads for the sake of securing his own forces. (5)
One should not enter an enemy's city or assembly unannounced;
one should wait for the right time for the sake of the task, and only depart when permitted.
He should know the strength of his kingdom, its fortresses and their protection, as well as the vulnerabilities of the enemy, along with the latter's treasury, allies, and army.
Even when weapons are raised, one should proclaim the teaching as it has been stated;
one should discern passion and its absence through the expressions of the eyes, the face, and physical gestures. (8)
One should avoid harsh speech, as well as desire and anger, even if they are accompanied by a reason.
One should not sleep with others; one should guard one's own disposition and understand the state of mind of another. ||9||
He should discern the loyalty and disloyalty of his subjects toward their master,
and he should carry out secret instigation among the faction of those who can be won over, remaining unobserved.
Even when being struck, he should not speak of any lapse in the character of his master;
rather, he should say with humble words, "Your Honor knows everything. (11)
One should perform the fourfold praise on both fortnights, [extolling the Buddha] for his preeminence in lineage, name, wealth, and deeds. (12)

By associating with those who receive wages from both sides under the pretext of teaching sciences or crafts, one should discern the faction of the enemy's agents as well as the movements of their master. 13.
For the sake of knowledge of the scriptures, he should frequent sacred fords, hermitages, and temples of the gods, together with his own spies who are disguised as ascetics. (14)
One should proclaim before those who can be divided the master’s majesty, lineage, sovereignty, generosity, excellence of exertion, nobility, and skillfulness. (15)
One who is asleep or intoxicated speaks of a hidden intention that has become manifest;
therefore, one should always sleep alone and avoid women and drink. (16)
As time passes, the wise person should not become despondent in the pursuit of accomplishing his goals;
he should recognize when time is being wasted through various forms of distraction.
As these days pass by, does he perceive some misfortune regarding our lord of the earth there, or does he intend to act himself? (18)
Or perhaps, as one most skilled in statesmanship, he may wish to quell internal unrest, or to gather in crops and other provisions, or to carry out fortification works within the citadel. (19)
Desiring the prosperity of his own side, he awaits the proper place and time; or perhaps he intends to launch an expedition himself, which is why he does not strive against us. (20)
Whether seeking to depart or awaiting the time of death, he may delay there;
however, when the time is being wasted, a wise man should reflect thus: (21)
Having clearly recognized any failure regarding the time for action, he should withdraw;
or, while remaining, he should report all matters concerning specific news to his master.
The identification of the enemy, the alienation of friends and kinsmen, knowledge of the fortresses, treasury, and army, and the winning over of those who can be won over. ||23||

The bringing under one's own control of the protectors of the kingdom, the wilderness, and the frontiers, as well as knowledge of the terrain for retreat in battle, is proclaimed as the duty of the envoy. (24)
A king should investigate his enemies through an envoy alone, and he should likewise ascertain the activities of foreign envoys within his own realm. (25)
The section on the activities of spies:

A spy should be one who understands logic and gestures, possesses a good memory, is gentle, moves with agility, endures hardship and fatigue, is skillful, and is possessed of quick understanding. (26)
Deceitful spies, bearing the outward marks of ascetics and subsisting on their crafts as merchandise,
should move about everywhere, drinking in the opinions of the world.
Every day, spies who are knowledgeable in all affairs should go out and enter the presence of the king,
for his sight indeed travels far.
By means of the movement of subtle spies, one should observe the activities of the enemy;
for a lord of the earth who possesses the eyes of scouts remains awake even while sleeping. (29)
Like Vivasvat with his splendors and like the wind with its movements, the king should pervade the entire world through spies who are esteemed by the people. (30)
The king, whose eye is his intelligence, should advance by means of that [intelligence] to a great extent;
for by not advancing by this [means], he falls from the path like a blind man, even on level ground. (31)
One should learn of the accumulation of all the enemies' wealth, their activities in every situation, and their aspirations for that territory and so forth, by means of spies. (32)
The moving [class of beings] is traditionally held to be twofold: luminous and non-luminous.
This [latter] is designated as non-luminous; the luminous is called the messenger (dūta).
A wise man should proceed with care, like a priest following the ritual manual at a sacrifice;
for the maintenance of peace depends upon the envoy, and his conduct is the foundation of his mission.
The various stations, possessing specific configurations, should be established for the success of the mission, wherein the agents, well-versed in the conduct of others, may remain in motion. (35)

A merchant, a farmer, an ascetic, a mendicant, and likewise a teacher—these should be established as spies for the purpose of gathering intelligence, provided with their due allowances and living in comfort. (36)

Regarding whatever [points] may be intended, whether in one's own position or in the position of another, those who understand the mind should remain with their movement directed toward all of them. (37)
The sharp, the renunciant, the spy, and the poisoner—these are the primary agents, all of whom must remain ignorant of one another's activities. (38)
He who does not know what is intended by his own side or by the enemy's side, while awake among his foes, is as if asleep; he shall never wake again. (39)
One should recognize those who are angry toward their own possessions out of a specific cause;
however, one should subdue those wicked ones who are angry without cause by means of silent punishment.
But those who are angry for a specific cause, one should subdue them and then lie down;
one should pacify even the slightest opening in the enemy's mouth with gifts and honors. (41)
One should bring about the pacification of the kingdom by removing thorns through the suppression of their faces;
being diligent, one should employ conciliation and gifts, and fill up any vulnerabilities.
Having entered through even a minute opening, an enemy, though more powerful, may utterly submerge the kingdom, just as water fills a drinking vessel. (43)
Those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, or deaf; those in disguise; eunuchs; as well as Kirātas, dwarfs, hunchbacks, and artisans of that sort—[these are excluded]. ||44||
Bhikṣukīs, cāraṇas, female slaves, garland-makers, and artisans skilled in the arts may carry out news from within the inner apartments while remaining unobserved. ||45||
Those who carry the parasol, the fly-whisk, the water-pitcher, and the vehicles, as well as other similar persons, shall be the high officials (mahāmātras) who know external affairs. 46.
Those who prepare food and condiments, the cooks, as well as the bath-attendants, the decorators, the servers, and even those who massage the limbs; ||47||
Those who provide water, betel, flowers, perfumes, and ornaments, as well as those who give flavorful food and others who are nearby, should be appointed as providers of tastes. (48)
Through signs, foreign dialects, writings, gestures, and even bodily movements,
the spies should move about among one another with composure, conducting their secret operations.
Drinking in the thoughts of the world as the rays of the sun drink the waters of the earth,
they were proficient in the study of many arts.
And spies should move about, assuming many disguises and forms. ||50||
In whatever manner one who knows the high and the low might approach others for the sake of his own prosperity,
that very same manner should be applied by those who know it to themselves, with a mind established in well-being.
And one should know that it is being employed by another. ||51||
The Fourteenth Canto:
The Section on the Praise of Zeal.
When the efforts of the messenger have proved fruitless through his daily conduct and activities,
One should proceed by means of the vehicle as previously described, preceded by subtle intelligence. ||1||
When the intellect is firmly established through both subtle discernment and diligent effort, it indeed produces glorious fruit, just as the fire-drill produces fire. (2)
Just as gold is obtained from ore and clarified butter from churning [milk], so too a certain fruit results from resolute effort accompanied by intellectual application. (3)
The wise one, endowed with enthusiasm and possessed of perseverance, is the supreme vessel for glories, just as the great ocean is for waters. (4)
Prosperity is nurtured by the intellect, just as a lotus pond is sustained by an abundance of water;
it is brought to expansion through exertion and resolute determination. (5)
Fortune does not depart from the body of one who is endowed with perseverance and whose intellect is pure, just as a shadow does not leave it; rather, she increases in extent.
Great fortunes enter one who is free from calamity, unwearied, possessed of great energy and great intelligence, just as rivers flow into the lord of streams. (7)
Even though he possesses the intelligence of a sentient being, one whose mind is seized by calamity is despised by riches, just as a eunuch is by women; such a person is overcome by indolence.
One should increase one's strength through exertion, just as fire is increased by fuel;
for even a weak person who is constantly industrious attains prosperity.
One should always desire perseverance in order to enjoy prosperity—which is like a wicked woman—by means of personal effort; for one should certainly not act like a eunuch.
One who is ever-energetic and has adopted the conduct of a lion should bring prosperity under his control, just as one might seize a wicked woman by her hair. ||11||
Without placing his foot upon the heads of his enemies— heads adorned with the jewels of crowns and bearing protective amulets— a man does not attain prosperity.
Without uprooting the tree of the enemy that has taken root here by means of the great elephant of the mind, which must be driven with diligent effort, how can there be happiness? (13)
By his arms, which resemble the trunks of majestic elephants and are tawny with the rays of sharp swords flashing as they are drawn with ease, he brings forth glories.
The great man, desiring to rise higher and still higher, stretches out his steps.
The lowly person sinks lower still out of fear and suspicion of falling.
Even one who is vastly superior in strength, when presided over by great courage,
surely places his foot upon the head of a rutting elephant— just as a lion does.
Free from fear, he should display an appearance that inspires fear, like a serpent displaying its coils;
and according to his strength, he should inflict punishment upon the enemy. (17)
The section on the calamities of the constituents:
whatever calamity may arise concerning the constituents should be pacified and then addressed;
it arises through both policy and impolicy, and even from fate. (18)
Because it casts one away from what is beneficial, it is called a vice (*vyasana*); since one who is addicted to vice sinks lower and lower, one should therefore avoid it. (19)
Fire, water, disease, famine, and likewise pestilence—these are the five kinds of divine calamities; thereafter follows the human. (20)
One who knows the true nature of action should bring destiny to a state of peace through human effort and tranquility, and the human element through industriousness and prudent policy.
I shall now explain, in due order, the duties and the calamities pertaining to that natural circle of states (maṇḍala) which begins with the sovereign and ends with the enemy. ||22||
The mantra, the attainment of the fruit of the mantra, the performance of duties, the future, income and expenditure, the science of government (daṇḍanīti), and the warding off of enemies. ||23||
"The remedy for calamity and the protection of the king and the kingdom—this is the duty of a minister; yet one possessed by such calamities destroys it. (24)
For a king being led away by ministers who are themselves beset by calamities is truly unable to rise up, like a bird whose wings have been clipped. (25)
Gold, clothing, grain, and so forth, as well as vehicles and other collections of wealth,
indeed arise from progeny.
The people accomplish their livelihood through agriculture and trade; indeed, livelihood is the very support of the world.
When the people are in distress, nothing at all succeeds.

Providing protection for the subjects in times of calamity and maintaining the treasury and the army—the citizens indeed assist those who possess fortresses here in this world by providing refuge. (28)
Silent warfare, protection of the people, securing both friends and enemies, and the prevention of harassment by neighboring kings and forest tribes are achieved by taking refuge in a fort. (29)
A king stationed in a fortress is honored by both his own party and the opposing party;
for indeed, everything perishes through the calamity of losing that fortress. (30)
The maintenance of servants, giving gifts, decoration, the management of vehicles, steadfastness, counteracting the intrigues of others, and the fortification of the fortress itself. ||31||
The construction of embankments, commerce, the acquisition of subjects and friends, and the accomplishment of dharma, pleasure, and wealth—all these proceed from the treasury. (32)
"The king has his treasury as his root"—this is a proverb known throughout the world;
a king who suffers the loss of his treasury quickly abandons all of this. (33)
A protector of the earth who possesses a treasury increases his depleted strength and naturally wins over his subjects; even by enemies, he is sought after for support. (34)
The winning over of friends, enemies, gold, and lands;
the swift execution of tasks that are distant; and the protection of what has been acquired. (35)
The destruction of enemy armies and the maintenance of one's own army proceed from this [punishment];
in its failure, they go to ruin. (36)
For even enemies certainly become friends for one who wields the rod of punishment;
indeed, a king who relies primarily on punishment enjoys the earth by means of conquest. (37)
He consolidates his friends and even eradicates his enemies;
through his land, treasury, and army, he renders assistance even with his very life. (38)
Externally, he performs various acts of affection and forms bonds of friendship;
yet when that person falls into misfortune, no duty of a friend is found in him. (39)
Even without being asked for assistance, a friend quickly stands by one's welfare;
possessing such a friend, one accomplishes even difficult goals without effort. (40)
The critical examination of the sciences, the protection of the virtuous social orders and stages of life, the mastery of weapons and treatises, and training in the methods of warfare; ||41||
Physical exercise, proficiency in weapons, the characteristics of armor, and the proper management of elephants, horses, and chariots. 42.
Skill in wrestling, the power of illusion, and the ability to enter another's mind; roguishness toward those who are deceitful, and the display of virtuous conduct toward the righteous. (43)
The application of mantras, the state of being consecrated by them, their protection, and abiding therein;
equanimity, conciliation, generosity, sowing dissension, and force—these are the means of accomplishment. ||44||
The thorough knowledge of the activities of the Praśāstṛ, Sūta, Senānī, Mantrin, Amātya, and Purohita, as well as the removal of those who are wicked. ||45||

The thorough knowledge of what has been done and what remains to be done, the dispatching of envoys, the removal of calamities affecting the constituent elements of the state, and the pacification of those who are enraged; ||46||
Following the instructions of gurus, honoring those worthy of worship, establishing the seat of Dharma, and purging the thorns from the kingdom. ||47||

He should have full knowledge of those who are supported and those who are not, an examination of what has been done and what remains undone, and a consideration of the satisfaction or dissatisfaction of all his dependents. (48)
Knowledge of the conduct of those who are neutral and middling, the protection of their success, the acceptance of friends, and the subjugation of enemies. ||49||
The protection of sons, wives, and so forth, the maintenance of the circle of kinsmen, and the promotion of one's own livelihoods such as mines, elephants, and forests; ||50||
The rejection of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous; non-violence toward all living beings and the avoidance of unrighteous acts. ||51||
The prohibition of improper actions and the promotion of proper deeds; the giving of what should be given and the non-retention of what should not be given. ||52||

Non-punishment of those who should not be punished, and the punishment of those who deserve it; likewise, the non-seizure of those who should not be seized, and the seizure of those who should be seized. ||53||
The performance of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful, the collection of taxes according to justice, and the remission of them by oneself; ||54||
The support of the principal [ministers], the removal of those who are unworthy, the pacification of irregularities, and the non-opposition of the servants; ||55||
The understanding of what is not yet understood, the ascertainment of what has been understood, the constant initiation of action, and seeing the conclusion of what has been begun. (56)
The desire to obtain what has not yet been obtained by righteous means, the increase of what has been obtained, and the formal bestowal of what has increased upon a worthy recipient. ||57||
The prohibition of unrighteousness, conduct according to the path of justice, and the mutual relationship between benefactor and beneficiary—this is the proper conduct of a lord of the earth. (58)
A king who is diligent and guided by statesmanship leads all these, beginning with his ministers, to prosperity; however, one who is addicted to vice leads them only to ruin. (59)
While he is thus preoccupied with matters of dharma and worldly affairs, and likewise unsettled in mind, the minister, being wise, ought to lead him through all of this in detail. (60)
The section on the vices of nature:
harshness of speech and punishment, as well as the misappropriation of wealth; drinking, women, hunting, and gambling—these are the vices of a king. (61)
Laziness, obstinacy, arrogance, negligence, and the inciting of enmity—these, as previously taught, are recorded as the vices of a minister. (62)
Excessive rain, drought, mice, locusts and the like, disrespect, punishment, foreign armies, and thieves. (63)
The execution of beloved ones by the king's army, the affliction of pestilence and disease, and the death or sickness of livestock—this is called a calamity for the kingdom. (64)

The state of having ruined machines, ramparts, and moats, as well as being unarmed, is called a calamity of the fort, resulting from the exhaustion of its defensive weapons, fuel, and provisions. (65)
Expenditure, depletion, consumption, lack of accumulation, as well as being plundered and situated at a distance— these are called the calamities of the treasury.

One who is besieged, one who is surrounded, one who has been insulted, one who has not been honored, one who is unpaid, one who is diseased, one who is exhausted, one who has come from afar, and one who has newly arrived. (67)
It is utterly exhausted, obstructed, and likewise its foremost momentum destroyed;
it is filled with the void of hope and has indeed attained falsehood.

Likewise, one who has been cast out by his wife or by his mother-in-law, as well as one with an internal thorn, one whose fetus has perished, one who has fled, and likewise one who has been abandoned. ||69||

One who has an angry enemy close at hand, one who is settled among enemies, one who is joined with seditious elements, one who is distracted by his own people, and likewise one who is distracted by his allies; ||70||
With its supply routes and reinforcements cut off, likewise with its base rendered empty, deprived of its master’s presence, and likewise with its defensive positions broken; ||71||
A calamity of the army that has a difficult rear-guard and is blind is said to be of two kinds:
some of these are incurable, while others are curable. ||72||
But one who is besieged should fight after emerging from another [direction] with superior force;
however, one who is surrounded on all sides should not attempt to escape when there is no path.
For one who has been honored and provided with the fulfillment of his desires and wealth will fight;
but one who is excessively insulted will have the fire of his wrath ignited.

One should fight even if not paid excessively, provided one has received wages for that time; however, one who is diseased and incapable of action should not be fought, for a diseased person is easily overcome.
For one who is exhausted should fight, while one who is rested should be well-provided for;
one who has traveled a long distance and whose life-force is spent is incapable of grasping a weapon. (76)
For one should lead a newly arrived force to fight, mixed with the local inhabitants;
however, once its chief heroes have been slain and it is utterly exhausted, it will no longer fight. (77)
For when it has been repulsed and joined with great heroes, its foremost strength destroyed, it is no longer capable of crushing those before it. ||78||
One who has attained their goal through hope and disillusionment does not fight for the fulfillment of that hope;
for one who is not established on the ground cannot advance when the earth is obstructed by its own narrowness.

One should fight against one who has arrived untruthfully, provided one possesses appropriate weapons and vehicles; likewise, one should fight against one who has brought along his wife or is accompanied by a pregnant woman, as such a person is incapable of enduring battle.
That which is separated by many kingdoms and cast far away does not fight;
for that which has the thorn of an enemy within is indeed intolerable, being pierced by an internal sting. (81)

That which is separated from one another, whose internal cohesion is broken, does not fight; likewise, even if capable, that which has withdrawn or is encompassed by another kingdom [does not fight]. (82)
That army which has been abandoned and its leaders have fled is not fit for battle;
however, that hereditary force of one's father and grandfather, though enraged, is capable of being pacified.
An ally situated together with enemies is incapable due to being overwhelmed by them; likewise, one stationed near the enemy is incapable of fighting because of the enemy's superior power. (84)
Having removed those who are to be corrupted, he should fight once the thorns have been pulled out;
protected by his principal warriors, he should advance while still accompanied by the corruptible.
That which is "thrown by oneself" is declared to be thrown within one's own domain;
that which is "thrown by a friend" is ineffective because of the extreme distance of place and time. (86)
The supply of grain and other provisions is called *vīvadha*, while reinforcements from friends are called *āsāra*.
An army whose supplies and reinforcements are cut off is not fit for battle. (87)

Indeed, it is not fitting for him to leave his ancestral and hereditary capital empty; however, once the protection of the countryside has been secured, it is appropriate to leave the capital empty during battle. (88)

For that which is protected by the root [of the lineage] fights with effort against what is empty at its root; yet it does not fight at all against that which is devoid of a master, being separated from its master. (89)

One should not fight an army whose vanguard is broken, which is leaderless, which is tormented by internal dissension from behind, which is difficult to attack in the rear, and which is incapable. (90)
For that which is without a guide is considered blind; because of its delusion, it is incapable of action.
Observing such "calamities of strength" and so forth, one should rise up against it. (91)
A friend who is oppressed by fate, seized by the forces of an enemy, and beset by the aforementioned faults arising from desire and anger; ||92||

Regarding the seven constituent elements beginning with the king that have been previously enumerated, it is said that among them, each preceding one is more serious in its misfortune than the following. (93)
Thus, a king should diligently understand all these calamities of the *prakṛtis* as they truly are;
and with both intelligence and power, he should counteract such calamity.
That is the removal [of the vow] at the proper time. ||94||
One who desires prosperity should not neglect the calamities of the constituent elements out of negligence or pride;
for he who neglects the calamities of the constituent elements [perishes].
Before long, his enemies are utterly defeated. ||95||
Thinking "this and this must certainly be accomplished through right action," one who strives should bring [the goal] to fruition;
he whose group of subjects has its vulnerabilities closed by sound policy.
That lord of the earth enjoys the three aims of life for a long time.
Fifteenth canto:
The section on the group of seven vices.
The constituent elements of sovereignty, beginning with the ministers and ending with the allies, are called the kingdom.
The misfortune of a king is more grievous than all other calamities of a kingdom. (1)
But a king who is free from vice is capable of dispelling the calamities of his kingdom;
for a kingdom, however powerful, is not capable of dispelling the calamities of its king. (2)
That king who is able to extricate his own self, ministers, subjects, forts, treasury, army, and allies from calamities partakes in the three aims of life.
A king who lacks the eye of the treatises is called blind;
better is the blind man than the one with eyes who, through intoxication, has cast aside the true path.
A blind man is led upon the path by ministers skilled in counsel;
but one who possesses sight, being blinded by intoxication, does not destroy himself entirely. ||5||
Therefore, a king who possesses the eye of the treatises, remaining steadfast in the counsel of his high ministers,
should abandon those vices that obstruct dharma and artha.
Harshness of speech and punishment, as well as the misappropriation of wealth—these three vices born of anger have been declared by those who know the true nature of vices. (7)
Hunting, gambling, women, and likewise drinking—these are declared by those who understand the nature of vices to be the fourfold addiction born of desire. (8)
Harsh speech causes great agitation in the world and is useless;
one should not utter unpleasant words, but should instead win people over to oneself.
The world trembles before one who, out of anger, suddenly utters much harsh speech, as if before a fire emitting sparks. (10)
The sharp sword of speech, falling repeatedly upon the heart, cuts the vital organs;
when it blazes, it inflames the spirited man and turns him into an enemy.
A king should not distress the world; he should be pleasant-spoken rather than harsh.
For generally, even a miser is served if his speech and actions are agreeable.
The punishment that establishes what has not yet been established is called "instruction" by the wise;
one should administer that punishment through reason alone, for one who applies punishment with reason is praised. (13)
A king who employs harsh punishment terrifies living beings;
and living beings, being thus terrified, seek refuge with his enemies. (14)
Even enemies, when supported by the people, attain prosperity; and once prosperous, they lead to destruction. Therefore, one should not cause distress to the subjects. 15.
Kings who act for the benefit of the world flourish;
through the prosperity of the world comes the prosperity of kings, and when it declines, they too perish. (16)
Even for great offenses, one should avoid the death penalty;
except in the case of seizing the kingdom, a proportionate punishment is praised.
For those who know the principles of policy, the abandonment of a great wealth for the sake of corrupting a corruptible object is called "corruption of wealth" (arthadūṣaṇa). //18//
Therefore, one who constantly desires his own welfare should not, when suddenly overcome by an exceedingly powerful anger, bring about the ruin of his purpose.
The jolting of the vehicle, the falling of the vehicle, and likewise the overturning of the vehicle; as well as the affliction of hunger, thirst, fatigue, exhaustion, cold, wind, and heat. (20)
Through the success of their expedition, they experienced the great suffering born of calamities on the journey—lands of scorched sand, kusha grass, and thorns. (21)
Dangers arising from dense thickets of trees, being torn by creepers and thorns, falling from mountains, being struck by masses of stones, stumps, or anthills; ||22||
In mountain caves, river valleys, and forest depths, they suffer the afflictions of slaughter and imprisonment by neighboring kings, forest-dwellers, and others who lie in wait. (23)
One's own armies and kinsmen, as well as those alienated by others, will bring about one's death;
likewise, there shall be fear of bears, pythons, elephants, lions, tigers, and the like. (24)

The obstruction caused by the smoke of forest fires, confusion regarding the directions, and wandering aimlessly—these and other such things are recorded as the vices of hunting for lords of the earth. (25)

Exhaustion is overcome through physical exercise, which results in the depletion of fat, phlegm, and toxins; furthermore, there is unsurpassed mastery in hitting both moving and stationary targets with arrows. (26)
Others claim these are the virtues of hunting, but that is not appropriate;
for the most part, its faults are life-threatening. Therefore, one should avoid it. (27)
For the *āmā* and other humors undergo digestion by means of their own appropriate [processes] day and night; and mastery in archery arises with respect to moving targets. (28)
If, however, he has a desire for the sport of hunting, he should have a charming hunting forest established near the city for the sake of recreation.
It was surrounded by a moat impassable even for wild animals,
measuring half a yojana in both length and circumference.
On the slopes of a mountain or by a river, where there is sufficient water and lush grass, free from thorny creepers and shrubs, and devoid of poisonous trees. ||31||
It was graced by well-known trees that bestowed flowers and fruit, captivating to the mind, and possessing sparse yet lush, dark, and dense shade. (32)
Its chasms, ravines, and caves were filled with dust until they were without gaps; its ground was leveled with crushed stumps, anthills, and stones. ||33||
Its waters were purified of crocodiles, its reservoir was not deep, it was strewn with various flowers, and frequented by various birds. ||34||
It was filled with well-tamed deer and accompanied by female elephants and their calves;
it was free of snakes with broken fangs and claws, and of horned animals with severed horns.
It was encircled by forest ranges growing on the banks of moats, entwined with flowering creepers and vines that were pleasant to touch.
