With its trees, pillars, and ground extending far into the distance, it was inaccessible to enemy armies and increased the joy of the mind. (37)
Likewise, for the prosperity of kings, it was guarded by trusted guards who were knowledgeable of the minds of forest-dwellers, capable of enduring the exhaustion of affliction, and steadfast. (38)
To that end, the king’s people, having overcome all fatigue, shall introduce various species of wild animals here for his diversion. (39)
Without conflicting with other duties, the king should enter for recreation in the morning, accompanied by a limited number of trusted attendants, provided he is fit for walking.
And when the king enters outside for the sake of recreation,
then the army, fully equipped and stationed with great care, should remain within a range both near and far.
Whatever virtues the virtuous have rightly proclaimed regarding the pursuit of hunting, a king who delights in the sport shall obtain them all therein. (42)
This is the prescribed rule for the excellent sport of hunting;
otherwise, a king should not go hunting like a mere hunter. (43)
Even from great wealth comes destruction, the loss of shame, lack of truthfulness, cruelty, anger, and the shattering of speech like a weapon. (44)
Greed is the neglect of religious duties, the non-performance of prescribed actions, the severing of association with the virtuous, and dwelling together with the wicked. ||45||
The inevitable destruction of wealth, constant persistence in enmity, hopelessness even when wealth exists, and hopefulness even when it does not exist. (46)
At every moment there is anger and joy, at every moment there is distress, and at every moment there is affliction; at every moment, there is the questioning of witnesses. (47)
Disregard for bodily refinements such as bathing and other enjoyments;
lack of physical exertion; weakness of the limbs; and reflection upon the meaning of the scriptures. ||48||
The concealment of urine and excrement, and the affliction of hunger and thirst—those skilled in the treatises declare these and others to be the vices of gambling. (49)
But the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja, like another world-protector, was deprived of his wife and other possessions while playing with fraudulent dice. (50)
And King Nala, when his great prosperity had been lost at dice,
abandoned his lawful wife in the forest and became a servant to others.
Equal on earth to the lord of the world, he who had no rival among archers—
that Rukmī, radiant as a mountain of gold, has come to ruin through the vice of gambling.
Even Dantavaktra, the dull-witted king of the Kāśikas and Ruśas, suffered the breaking of his own teeth due to the grave fault of being addicted to gambling. (53)
From gambling arises a fury for misfortune; from gambling comes the great destruction of affection;
and from gambling, the division of even the greatest factions proceeds. (54)
Thus, a king should avoid gambling, which consists solely of faults; and a wise ruler should likewise prohibit betting matches among the arrogant.
The wasting away of time for tasks, the oppression of dharma and artha,
the provocation of those of virtuous nature due to constant internal presence,
the betrayal of secrets, and subsequently, the engagement in improper acts. 56.
Envy, resentment, anger, hostility, and acts of rashness; ||57||
And so forth; whatever has been previously proclaimed regarding the vice of women, therefore a king who desires his kingdom should abandon the vice of women. (58)
The endeavors of those small-minded men who are distracted by gazing upon the faces of women come to an end here along with their youth. (59)
Vomiting, agitation, loss of consciousness, nakedness, much incoherent prattle, and sudden, repeated misfortune; ||60||
Exhaustion of vital energy, loss of friends, confusion of wisdom, learning, and intellect; separation from the virtuous, association with the wicked, and encounter with misfortune. ||61||
Stumbling, trembling, lassitude, and excessive devotion to women—such are the evils of drinking, which are utterly condemned by the virtuous. (62)
Endowed with learning, virtue, and strength, the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, despite being known as "the imperishable," went to their destruction through excessive addiction to drink.
But the blessed Śukra, the lord of yogis, whose intellect was equal to that of Bhṛgu,
drank the potent draught and consumed his own legitimate son as a disciple.
For a person impelled by drink acts here and there; because of acting here and there, he incurs the state of being unfit for social intercourse. (65)
One may indeed indulge in women or drink moderately;
however, a wise man should not engage in gambling or hunting, for they are extreme vices.
This noble vice, which creates obstacles to all that is beneficial, has been taught here as being of seven kinds by those who know the method for its removal;
for through addiction, it brings about destruction instantly and in a single stroke.
Why, then, would he not be the slayer by virtue of their simultaneous arising? ||67||

It causes the senses to lose their capacity for enjoyment; it destroys even what has been heard, as well as excellence and preeminence; for it shakes even the greatest prosperity from its foundation. (36)
Even for those of wise intellect, this sevenfold [set] is difficult to overcome. || 68 ||
Foes surely despise those who are situated in calamity, and they become difficult to overcome;
however, the wise, when free from misfortune, [overcome] their enemies.
They treat others with contempt and become difficult to break. ||69||
The sixteenth canto: The section on the appearance of those who incite to expedition;
[the king] being free from various kinds of calamities.
Endowed with an incomparable triad of powers, a king desiring victory should march against an enemy who is beset by severe calamities. (1)
Generally, when enemies fall into calamity, the virtuous advise that one should march against them; in this regard, the following position holds: for calamity is indeed transient.
For one who is patient, having risen up, should indeed advance. ||2||
When one is able to forcibly strike down even a powerful enemy through prowess,
then indeed one should march forth to accomplish those harmful deeds.
Or causing pain and emaciation to another. ||3||
A king should march against the territory of another when its crops are ripe, crushing it for the sake of victory;
for by the destruction of the crops, the enemy's livelihood is destroyed.
The destruction [of the enemy] and the reinforcement of one's own army are excellent. ||4||
With a pure rear, searching ahead for dangerous places, skilled in the maneuvers of others, and having cleared the path of his own supplies and reinforcements;
May he, remaining vigilant, enter the earth [to slay] his enemies. ||5||
Whether on level ground or uneven terrain,
in low-lying areas or on high ground, a wise man who is free from illness and fearless should travel by his own power.
With his army equipped for battle and provided with food and water. ||6||
In the summer, one should travel along a path for elephants that has abundant water,
for the sake of providing relief from the heat produced by the summer season in the absence of water.
The elephant-like diseases come to be. ||7||
For even in elephants that are in good health,
heat indeed blazes within their bodies;
and it increases further through the application of exertion.
His majesty forcibly slays elephants. || 8 ||
Indeed, all sentient beings reach a state of extreme distress during the hot season without water,
their bodies being scorched by excessive heat.
The elephants, not drinking, depart immediately. ||9||
Upon elephants whose splendor was like that of dark clouds, who emitted sprays from the flow of fragrant ichor and whose tusks shattered the rocks upon impact.
The sovereignty of the lords of the earth is firmly established.
It was prepared for battle by that most heroic man who had mastered the path;
it was likewise well-attended by the horses that had been readied.
A single elephant slays six thousand. ||11||
Whether in water or on land, amidst a thicket of trees, on even or uneven ground, whether moving or stationary,
and even when breaking through walls, palaces, or towers;
Victory is certain for those who possess the strength of the Nāgas. ||12||
Therefore, one should march from wherever the path has abundant water, where there is an untroubled supply of food and drink,
thereby generating prestige.
Gradually resting the forces.
Even a slight provocation against those who are highly exalted may later incite a great wrath among enemies; therefore,
one should proceed after observing them with vigilance.
One should not destroy what is seen for the sake of the unseen. ||14||
Retaliation later and fruit first, or retaliation first and fruit later— of these two, retaliation first is more serious;
for when one is provoked, that very vulnerability becomes a great weakness.
Therefore, one should set out after having made a formal arrangement. ||15||
When one is capable both before and after,
then one should advance for the sake of great fruit;
for advancing with a pure front while the rear is impure leads to failure.
Indeed, he incurs a severe injury to the heel. ||16||
When about to depart, one should station a force that is divided into many units and has many leaders to guard the city ahead;
for where there are many leaders, there is no unanimity of opinion.
It has many leaders and is impenetrable by enemies. ||17||
Being intent on the necessity of departing, yet fearing a subsequent attack due to provoked hostility,
he [should send] either the commander-in-chief or the prince.
One should place [the vessel] in front with a portion of its strength. ||18||
Between internal and external provocation, the internal is indeed more serious;
having seized [the enemy], one should depart before he can move outside.
And having made the external [elements] beneficial for the purpose prescribed. //19//
The family priest, the ministers, the princes, and the kinsmen are the chief protectors of the army;
for among these, the provocation of even one leads to ruin.
They teach the internal provocation [of the elements]. ||20||

An external uprising among the border-guards, forest-dwellers, or those on the frontiers constitutes one of the types of external provocation; when it arises, it should be addressed through skillful means of surveillance.
He should properly employ him with the assistance of his ministers. ||21||
One should pacify provocation through conciliation and other means, as well as by mutual restraint and sowing dissension;
likewise, a wise person should thus subdue a mental affliction.
So that they may divide [the property] without causing distress to others. ||22||
The depletion of human labor and draft animals is indeed loss; the depletion of gold and grain is expenditure.
Therefore, one of clever intellect should not [spend] this.
One should resort to that which causes exhaustion, loss, and toil. ||23||
One should undertake that which is certain to be accomplished, rich in great fruit, free from procrastination, and conducive to ultimate transformation,
even if it involves expense and exertion.
But one should never [speak] that which is characterized by the fault of exhaustion. ||24||
Exertion toward things that are impossible, exertion at the wrong time toward things that are possible,
and failing to exert oneself toward things that are possible due to delusion.
They say that the failure of an undertaking is indeed threefold. ||25||
Lust, intolerance, lack of courtesy, compassion, shame, fear, cruelty, ignobility,
hypocrisy, arrogance, and even excessive piety—
The wretchedness of one's own group and the humiliation [they suffer]. ||26||
Betrayal, fear, constant negligence, and intolerance of cold, heat, and rain—
these are brought upon one by time.
They certainly create obstacles to spiritual accomplishment. ||27||
Then there is the natural friend, the acquired friend, the friend by birth, and the friend arising from business;
and the servant who is maintained with various forms of hospitality.
The wise declare that the side [of existence] is sevenfold. ||28||
By constant following, by proclaiming virtues, by enduring censure, by guarding against faults,
and by efforts for his sake, by purity, and by discussions concerning him.
It should be understood that the partisan is one who is full of attachment. ||29||
One who is of noble birth, noble, learned, disciplined, elevated by self-respect, refined, of unshakeable intellect,
and endowed with gratitude, vigor, wisdom, and fortitude.
One should indeed know that [the king] as one who belongs to the side of good conduct. ||30||
Diligence, intelligence, fortitude, courage, truthfulness, renunciation, affection, steadfastness, dignity,
mastery over the senses, endurance, and modesty.
Boldness is the preeminent among the qualities of the self. ||31||

They say that the power of counsel consists of the efficacy of mantras and the application of sound policy; the power of the treasury and the army is called the power of sovereignty; and the power of energy is the vigorous exertion of force.
Endowed with the three powers, he becomes a conqueror in this world. ||32||
Quickness, great dexterity, lack of despondency in calamities,
extreme fortitude amidst successes,
and intuition arising from the study of the scriptures.
Cognition arising from association is also subject to transformation. (33)
Zeal, courage, determination, exertion, firmness in actions, and human effort here,
as well as freedom from disease and the attainment of the fruits of action— [these constitute success].
Favorability of fate and freedom from disease. ||34||
Having secured his treasury by means of this [strategy] beginning with "wings" (*pakṣa*),
he should advance against an enemy who is deprived of wings;
thus advancing, he will surely reach the ocean.
He obtains that earth cleansed [of all impurities]. ||35||
The time for elephants to travel is when the sky is covered with clouds like a mass of water; for horses, it is any other time,
provided it is not excessively rainy, hot, or frosty.
"But with crops fully ripened" refers to the excellence of the season. //36//
At night the owl destroys the crows,
and at the end of the night the crow destroys the owls;
thus, one should march after carefully observing the proper time.
In due time, one's desired goals bear fruit in this world. ||37||
The dog drags the crocodile standing on the bank,
and the crocodile drags the dog who has entered the water; as they both struggle, each inevitably comes to grief.
Abiding in its own place, it experiences the fruit of karma. ||38||
Level ground for horses and uneven terrain for elephants, as well as water-abundant areas for boats and mountainous regions for those followed by infantry forces.
And having carefully considered [the situation] according to one's strength, [one should offer] a mixture. ||39||
In this world, one may fall into water that is deep as the heavens,
or during the summer into a forest thicket near water that is difficult to traverse;
having observed both these mixed conditions, one should act according to what is comfortable.
The lord of men went to the country for victory. ||40||
Neither too much water nor lacking water, properly supplied with fodder and fuel,
having reached a road frequented by many who know it well—
One should approach the enemy with ease during military expeditions. ||41||
One should approach the enemy's territory only with one's own supplies and essential provisions,
with water available, with people who have been inspired by confidence,
and remaining pure.
For one who is afflicted should not retreat. ||42||
Those fools who rashly undertake a long journey against their enemies without examining the terrain fall,
before long, under their swords.
The embrace of the stream is easily accomplished without effort. ||43||
And on the road, the one skilled in ritual procedures, having duly provided protection for his army stationed in a difficult position,
stood with heroic warriors ready at his side.
One should practice the auspicious yogic sleep at night. ||44||
With the cavities of his ears filled by the neighing of wandering horses and the trumpeting of lordly elephants,
he nevertheless remained within that state, possessed of awakened awareness.
One should pay heed to those who ask, "Who are awake? ||45||
Then, having awakened, pure and with his tutelary deity worshipped, resplendent with glorious ornaments and filled with joy,
he was attended by the foremost ministers in the prescribed manner.
And together with the groups of domestic priests, ministers, and friends. ||46||
Having deliberated with them on what ought to be done, he mounted his magnificent vehicle,
accompanied by warriors of noble birth who were like his own self.
He should go outside, surrounded [by his retinue]. ||47||
The king may observe the movement of elephants, chariots, and horses,
as well as the collective body of warriors and their individual units;
he may also inspect the selected elephants twice a day.
And also horses equipped according to the rules. ||48||
Easy to approach, speaking with a smile, he should say what is pleasant and give more than required for his livelihood;
those who are gathered by such kindness and generosity [will remain loyal].
They would even give up their lives for their husband. ||49||
He should be fit for vehicles such as chariots, horses, boats, and elephants;
he should perform his daily duties and be proficient in archery,
even in tasks difficult for those of keen intellect.
It bestows skill in constant practice. ||50||
Mounted upon a highly caparisoned elephant,
followed by an array of armored troops,
he performed a virtuous consultation with the envoy of the vassal king.
He should march while screened by brave warriors. ||51||
He should observe the movements of his enemies through spies and envoys endowed with the qualities of intelligence;
for a lord of the earth who is deprived of these becomes [vulnerable].
He shares the same nature as both people and those without eyes. ||52||
Enticing him by giving even a little,
one should win over the frontier-guard of the enemy;
one should constantly supply goods from one's own kingdom to the enemy.
One should take the beneficial merchandise by means of the tube. ||53||
One who is concluding a treaty should swiftly carry out the desired preliminary action upon the arrival of the envoy; if, however,
the treaty is not concluded, he alone remains there.
And one's own self-exaltation is thereby accomplished. ||54||
One should win over the forest-dwellers and frontier guards along the roads even with gifts and conciliation; for when there is a siege in hostile territories, they are essential.
For they are his instructors in the path. ||55||
For whatever man, whether without cause or for some reason,
serves an enemy and, having become estranged from his own kin, approaches an adversary;
Whoever comes, one should observe his course.
One who intends to undertake an enterprise must first conduct a thorough investigation while endowed with the power of counsel;
for the power of counsel is weightier than the strength of arms.
Śakra conquered the asuras by the power of his spells.

One who understands the principles of policy, having perceived through pure discernment that the exertion of effort toward action leads to its fruit, should undertake it at the proper time and not let the opportunity pass.
For a fruit that is out of season is inevitably cast away. ||58||
The divine splendor of those high-souled ones— who are distinguished by their majesty, endowed with learning and valor, and who walk the path as it has been correctly beheld— endures for a long time.
It hangs from arms as long as serpents. ||59||

At a time when the harvests are abundant with the full perfection of men, when the mud has been cleared from the waters, and when one’s livelihood is diligently applied— as if in a forest blazing with the splendor of blossoming mango trees.
The lord of men should proceed well toward the enemy's territory for the sake of victory. ||60||
Thus, the king,
having applied his attention and being intent on attacking the enemy, should advance; for this is the result of following the prescribed rules.
It necessarily enters the range of that which has the nature of an adversary. ||61||
The Seventeenth Canto:
The Section on the Encampment of the Army.
Having approached the vicinity of the enemy’s city on ground approved by the wise, [he encamped].
One who knows how to establish a military camp should establish the camp. ||1||
It was square, with four gates, neither too wide nor too narrow, provided with battlements,
gate-towers, and walls, and surrounded by a great moat.
One should prepare a dwelling—either triangular, crescent-shaped, circular, or even oblong—according to the suitability of the site. (3)
It was provided with long, partitioned, and secluded side-wings;
it was well-guarded, shaped like a hollowed-out arm-pit, and surrounded by a great road.
In its center, one should have constructed a royal palace that delights the mind, surrounded by a great moat and provided with an inner treasury-chamber.
The hereditary, hired, guild, allied, enemy, and forest-dwelling forces should be stationed in order, surrounding the royal palace.
He should station within [the fort] his own men who are loyal, free from greed, proven in their actions, adequately paid, and trustworthy, along with the circle of neighboring kings.
Elephants that have received their names and horses as swift as thought should dwell near the king's residence, guarded by trusted attendants. (8)
For the protection of the king, the royal harem guard and the army should remain ready for battle day and night, well-equipped according to their assigned watches.
A great tusker fit for battle, fully equipped and well-mounted by its rider, and a swift horse, should stand at the gate of the king. (10)
A portion of the army, fully equipped and led by the commander-in-chief,
should vigilantly patrol outside in a circular formation during the night.
Those who are full of courage, swift-moving, mounted on wind-swift horses, and who roam the distant frontiers, shall ascertain the movements of the enemy forces. ||12||
At the gates, which were adorned with garlands hung from arches and equipped with mechanical flags, he should ensure the highest security through trusted agents.
Everyone should be observed as they go out and enter;
likewise, the messengers of others who come within the scope of the king's command should remain under surveillance. (14)
Restrained from idle clamor, laughter, gambling, and drinking, a person should remain with all necessary implements ready, intent upon every duty. (15)
Having left a passage for himself outside the trench for his own troops to move about, he should destroy the entire ground for the purpose of striking down the enemy army. ||16||
In some places he should defile the ground all around with thorny branches, in others with iron-tipped spears, and even with hidden pits.
In a place devoid of trees, shrubs, stones, stumps, anthills, and caves,
one should have military training grounds constructed using various types of equipment.
That country is considered excellent in which there are training grounds for the army according to one's desire, while for the enemy they are unfavorable; such is what has been heard. (19)
The grounds for exertion are equal for oneself and for others;
it is in this regard that the middle region has been designated by those who contemplate the meaning of the scriptures. (20)

A place where the ground is too extensive for the maneuvers of one's own army, yet suitable for the maneuvers of the enemy's host, and which is unfavorable to oneself, is considered the lowest type of terrain.
One should always desire the highest [state]; in its absence, the middling;
but for the sake of success, one should never resort to the lowest, which is the prison cell.
The chapter on the knowledge of signs:
as if assailed by some army of diseases, you are suddenly overcome by agitation, shrouded in a mist of dust. (23)
Suddenly, with harsh and greyish winds blowing, their banners fell;
mutual hostility arose among them, and the sound of their musical instruments ceased. ||24||
Inspiring fear and terror through mere imagination, marred by thunderclaps and meteors, vomiting forth blazing weapons, and accompanied by the inauspicious howling of jackals; ||25||
It was crowded with flocks of crows and vultures shrieking harshly,
repeatedly blazing with extreme ferocity, and drenched by rains of blood.
His royal star is afflicted by cruel, portentous planets; he sees headless trunks and other such omens in the sun's glare; and his mounts suddenly become bewildered. (27)
A military camp that is possessed of such deformities as an elephant in rut with its ichor completely dried up is not recommended. (28)
It was filled with joyful men and women, with drums resounding with auspicious sounds,
with horses neighing deeply, and with the trumpeting of honored elephants.
Rich with the sounds of the *puṇyāha* and the *brahman*, filled with dance and song, free from calamity, full of great enthusiasm, it brought joy to those who longed for it. (30)
Free from dust, it was showered with rain, and the planets remained in their favorable positions; it was devoid of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents. ||31||

With birds warbling auspiciously, with the cries of female jackals moving clockwise and favorably, with a gentle breeze blowing in a favorable direction, and with praises of auspiciousness being uttered. (32)
It was filled with joyful and well-nourished people, virtuous, fragrant, and ablaze with fire;
it possessed elephants in full rut and was attended by the rising of refreshing showers.
An army camp endowed with such characteristics as these is praised;
when it is auspicious, the enemy suffers defeat, but when it is inauspicious, the opposite should be known to occur. (34)
Since signs indicate the success or failure of ritual actions, one who desires his own welfare should therefore understand these signs according to their true nature. (35)
When an undertaking is begun with an auspicious omen and a pure inner self, that which is intended clearly attains success. (36)
Success belongs to him who possesses these: the excellence of companions, discernment, courage, favor from destiny, diligence, and resolve. (37)

Because he is the root of his subjects, the king is said to be the trunk; the retinue consisting of ministers, the army, and so forth, is called the enclosure, for the enclosure is defined as that which surrounds. (38)
Because the prosperity of beings is accomplished through a vast enclosure, and because it encloses the divisions [of the army], it is therefore known as a *skandhāvāra* (military camp). ||39||
Sudden assaults, the supply of fodder and water, and the interception of reinforcements—these must be guarded against with great effort, for they are the death of the camp. (40)
Thus, with diligent effort, he should station his forces and likewise observe their auspicious and inauspicious qualities;
he should also scrutinize these matters skillfully regarding the enemy.
One should undertake [the practice] when seeing those who have abandoned the unwholesome. ||41||
The Eighteenth Chapter:
The Section on the Varieties of Expedient Means.
Endowed with great wisdom and supported by his companions, [the Bodhisattva...]
Through exertion and resolve, one should apply strategic means against the enemy. ||1||
Setting aside the fourfold army, it is the treasury and counsel that fight; therefore, one who possesses sound counsel should conquer enemies through counsel and the treasury. (2)
Conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and punishment—these four, along with deception, indifference, and sorcery, are proclaimed as the seven expedients. (3)
The demonstration of mutual benefits, the proclamation of virtues, the declaration of the relationship, and the presentation of future prospects. ||4||
Gentle speech, and the offering [of gifts] with the words "I am yours"—thus, by those who know the methods of conciliation and dissension, conciliation is said to be fivefold. (5)
The relinquishing of wealth once it has been acquired—whether in superior, inferior, or middling measure—as well as its restitution or the rejoicing in what has been received; ||6||
The gift of material goods, the unprecedented [gift], the instigation of taking by oneself, and the relinquishing of what is to be given—giving is traditionally said to be fivefold. (7)
The removal of affection and passion, the incitement of rivalry, and likewise intimidation—these are known as the three types of sowing dissension by those skilled in creating division. ||8||
"Killing, the seizure of property, and likewise affliction—thus is punishment declared to be threefold by those who know the divisions of punishment. (9)
Punishment is said to be of two kinds: manifest and unmanifest.
One should inflict manifest punishment upon an enemy who is hated by the world. (10)
The world is terrified by those who are slain, even if they are favorites of the king; however, for those who cause excessive harassment, secret execution is recommended. (11)
By means of poison, secret applications, weapons, or ointments,
he should thus administer punishment in secret so that no one else may perceive it.
Whether it be a Brahmin who is merely so by birth, or even an outcaste who is righteous,
a wise person, desiring to uphold the Dharma, should not prescribe the punishment of execution.
Those who should be destroyed by indifference are praised for being dealt with secretly; yet a skillful person should avoid even such indifference in the presence of others. (14)
As if anointing their minds with his gaze, as if drinking them in well, and as if pouring forth nectar, he should employ the *sāman* and speak pleasant words. (15)
Speech that does not produce agitation is proclaimed as *sāman*;
the term *sāman* is also applied to that which is true, pleasant, soothing, dear, and a hymn of praise. (16)
As if selling his very self, he should give what is desired; like water, he should shatter his enemies unobserved, as if they were mountains.

Irresistible like one who holds a staff in hand, he should inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment; even when an offense is witnessed by his own eyes, he should act as if it were not witnessed. (18)
For the accomplishment of one's purpose, the wise man should strive with a disciplined mind;
the learned praise the attainment of conciliation above all else. (19)
The Ocean of Milk was churned with conciliation by the gods and demons for the sake of its fruit;
yet the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who were hostile to conciliation, were soon struck down.
A wise man should bring a terrible conflict to peace through generosity;
Indra brought about pacification through a gift when Śukra had offended him.
When the descendant of Bhṛgu was enraged at his daughter’s offense,
Vṛṣaparvan, the lord of the Dānavas, became happy through his gift.
Even by means of bribery, one who desires peace should give to the powerful;
Gāndhārī went to his destruction because he would not give, even though he possessed the root of all.
By offering something while enticing them with greater greed,
he should cause those who are susceptible to division to split into four groups, having infiltrated them through agents who receive wages from both sides.

One who has not received his wages yet is greedy; one who is proud but has been insulted; one who is angry but has been provoked suddenly; and likewise, one who is afraid but has been threatened. ||25||
One should win over these four types of people by means of desired objects;
one should likewise bring about their pacification among both the enemy faction and one's own faction as appropriate. ||26||
One should strive with effort to create dissension among the ministers, counselors, and priests;
for when they are divided, the powerful crown prince likewise becomes divided.
The minister and the crown prince are the two arms of the lord of the earth; the counselor is indeed his eye. Therefore, if he is divided from them, his death follows as well. (28)
But a wise man should transform one born of that family in every situation;
for one born of that family, when transformed, consumes his own kin like fire. (29)
But a man who has lived within [the enemy's camp] is equal to one born of that same lineage;
therefore, one should cause these two to be divided from the enemy and bring about peace for oneself. (30)
In that situation, one should employ instigation toward whoever is capable of both inciting anger and bestowing favor;
having examined whether such a person is well-disposed or treacherous, one should act with subtle intelligence. (31)
The virtuous person, however, makes his words bear fruit according to his ability;
the deceitful person, out of a desire for gain, wavers between both sides.

One who had previously been addressed with courtesy, yet was not treated with humility; one who was falsely accused, one who desired prosperity, and one who, having been summoned, was not honored. (33)
One who hates the king, one born of his family, one who is hated by the sovereign, one engaged in a lawsuit, and likewise one appointed to a judicial office; ||34||
One who is fond of battle, reckless, self-conceited, one whose virtue, pleasure, and wealth have been cut off, one who is angry, proud, and insulted; ||35||

One who is afraid, terrified by his own faults, one who has created enmity despite being excessively conciliated, one who is attached to an unequal person, and one who has been rejected by those of equal status; ||36||
Ceased without cause, and especially distinguished from those with causes;
abandoned without reason, he is worthy of worship yet remains unworshipped. (37)
Having had his wealth and wife taken away, longing for great enjoyments, he is utterly impoverished; with kinsmen cast out, his possessions stripped away, and himself excluded. ||38||
Thus have those to be divided been fully described; one should divide those who stand on the side of the enemy.
Those who have come over should be honored with desired objects, and one's own people should be brought to tranquility. (39)
Maintaining a common bond through shared desire, displaying extreme terrors, and employing superior gifts and honors—these are proclaimed as the means of sowing dissension. ||40||
A wise man, when attacked by one more powerful, should create a division;
having been split apart, the mighty Śaṇḍa and Marka were defeated by the gods. 41.
For by striking with force after breaking the enemy's compact army, it indeed falls apart like wood that has been split and eaten by woodworms. (42)
Endowed with enthusiasm, place, and time, and possessing excellent allies, one should utterly destroy enemies by means of punishment, just like Yudhiṣṭhira. (43)
Having observed one's own power, one may even employ force against a superior;
alone and endowed with power, Rāma formerly slew the Kṣatriyas. (44)
Lassitude, exhaustion from valorous exertion, the failure of strategic efforts, being tormented by loss, expense, and exile, and being utterly overwhelmed. (45)
One should win over a coward, a fool, a woman, a child, a righteous person, a wicked man, an animal,
one whose chief quality is friendship, and one of virtuous intent through conciliation.
One should bring a greedy person and one who is impoverished under control by means of gifts and by showing them honor;
likewise, one should subdue wicked people who have become divided by mutual suspicion by displaying the power of punishment.
One should win over sons, brothers, and kinsmen through conciliation and material gifts;
for who in this world is equal to these, even when they have been deeply offended? (48)
One should employ conciliation even toward those who have stumbled through the power of fate;
for the noble, being bound by their virtuous conduct, do not undergo transformation into something base even when faced with difficulties. (49)
Those in whom family, virtue, compassion, generosity, righteousness, truthfulness, gratitude, and lack of greed are found—these are called noble ones. (50)
An expert in the application of punishment should win over the citizens and the country folk, as well as the leaders of the army,
through gifts and sowing dissension, or others as appropriate.

A wise king should win over those of his own lineage who have been imprisoned, as well as the subordinate chieftains, by means of sowing dissension and punishment, or other appropriate methods as the case may require.
Men situated inside the hollows of pillars containing images of deities.
A man clothed in women's garments, a wondrous sight at night. ||53||
The similarity in form between vetālas, ulkā-piśācas, and gods—such illusions as these are to be recognized by the lords of men as being human in origin. (54)
Assuming forms at will, raining down weapons, missiles, stones, and water, as well as darkness, wind, mountains, and clouds—this is indeed superhuman illusion. (55)
Bhīma slew Kīcaka while relying on the form of a woman;
Nala remained in a concealed form for a long time through divine illusion.
Non-prevention of one who is engaged in an unjust cause, a calamity, or battle—thus indifference is declared to be threefold by those skilled in the meaning of indifference. (57)
But Kīcaka, who was intent on an improper act and whose vision was blinded by sensual objects, was ignored by Virāṭa with the thought, "Let him be killed. (58)
Agitated by Bhīmasena, Hiḍimbā—fearing the interruption of her own purpose—neglected her own brother, saying, "Let him be killed. (59)
There was the sight of clouds, darkness, rain, fire, mountains, and wonders;
and the sight of the armies standing at a distance, garlanded with banners.
One should display severed, split, and pierced [bodies] with blood flowing from them;
thus one should employ this "net of Indra" (illusion) for the purpose of terrifying enemies. 25–61.
Thus have the various means been fully described, which accomplish manifold purposes;
among them, one who knows the proper time should employ conciliation at the appropriate moment.
Conciliation and sowing dissension should be employed, preceded by gifts and honors;
for when joined with gifts, even these two lead to the accomplishment of one's purpose.
For one devoid of generosity, conciliation must be employed everywhere, even with a blade of grass; for conciliation without gifts does not find a foothold even among one's own wives.
Thus, one who knows policy should skillfully employ expedients against both his own forces and those of the enemy;
for one devoid of expedients is certain to fall into ruin.
Struggling, he approaches like one who is blind. ||65||
Prosperities inevitably come under the control of the wise through the power of the pincers of skillful means;
when applied according to rule, they become magnificent.
For the fruit [of action] for kings sometimes leads to the accomplishment of their aims. ||66||
The nineteenth canto: The section on the relative strength and weakness of the army,
concerning the failure of the three means beginning with conciliation (sāma).
Endowed with discipline and statesmanship, he who knows the proper application of punishment shall mete out punishment upon those deserving of it. ||1||
Having worshipped the gods and the brahmins under an auspicious constellation and planet,
and having arrayed his sixfold army, he should advance toward the enemy.
The army consists of hereditary troops, hired troops, guild troops, allies, enemy troops, and forest-dwelling troops;
among these forces, each preceding one is more important than the following, and likewise, their respective calamities are more serious. (3)
Due to honor, affection, and frequent conversation and sitting together, and because of being constantly permeated by their disposition, the hereditary army is more powerful than the hired force. (4)
Because of his constant proximity, his readiness to rise quickly, and because his livelihood depends upon the master, the hired servant is more powerful than the guild. (5)
The power of a guild is weighty because of mutual rivalry and resentment, as well as the attainment of happiness, strength, local support, and friendship. (6)

Because it involves countless places and times, because it pursues a single objective, and because it possesses the power to divide the enemy's forces, the strength of an ally is greater than that of an enemy. (7)
By nature they are unrighteous, greedy, ignoble, and destroyers of truth;
therefore, because of their forest-dwelling character, the enemy force is formidable against them.
Both of these are established as depending on time for the purpose of destruction;
whether in the case of destruction or in misfortune, his victory therein is certain. (9)
But there may be particular danger from one who acts as a sower of discord;
for by sowing discord among the enemy as well, victory is certain. (10)

An enemy who has been strengthened by his own hereditary subjects—who are prosperous, substantial, and loyal—should be marched against by one who is likewise [prosperous, substantial, and loyal], and who is capable of enduring loss and expense. (11)

One may travel on a distant route or for a long duration with the hereditary troops who are well-honored; for the hereditary troops, due to their long-standing service, are capable of enduring loss and expense. ||12||
In these matters, a wise person should avoid hiring servants and the like;
for among those who are exhausted by long journeys and time, there may arise the fear of dissension. (13)
Indeed, due to the very great number of troops, from exhaustion over a long period of time, and from constant marching and wandering, dissension will inevitably arise. (14)
My hired army is large, while my hereditary army is small and lacks substance; the enemy’s hereditary army is small or disaffected, and for the most part lacks substance. (15)
Generally, one should indeed fight by means of counsel, for it involves little effort;
moreover, the time required is short, the space occupied is small, and both loss and expenditure are minimal. (16)
If the enemy's army—or one's own—is confident because of the cessation of secret intrigues, one should approach with hired forces to strike down a small foraging party. (17)
A large guild-force can be employed for the purpose of transport;
since travel and exertion are short, one should mobilize with the guild. (18)
For a vast army of allies can be brought under one's own command; with little risk and through counsel, it is possible to achieve even greater exertion in battle. (19)
In a task that is common to both friends, where the emergence of the fruit depends upon the friend,
and in matters concerning a friend who is either to be favored or to be harmed, one should proceed together with that very friend.
One should fight great enemies with a vast army;
otherwise, like a dog or a pig seeking slaughter, one would meet his end like a low-born outcaste.
However, if the enemy's force is exceedingly powerful, one should station it near the foe out of fear of anger, and should weaken it by crushing its fortresses and thorns. 22.
A wise king should always place the forest-dwelling army at the forefront for clearing the thorns within his fort and for entering the territories of others. 23.
They know this fourfold army to have six divisions beginning with the *maula*;
it becomes sixfold when the counsel (*mantra*) and the treasury (*kośa*) are added to the infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants. (24)
Thus, having well-secured his own positions against vulnerabilities, the powerful king should advance against the enemy's force, employing these six kinds of power as appropriate. (25)
O King, the monarch should thoroughly understand this yoga of his general through all means, such as secret counsel, as well as everything done or left undone by him and the conduct of the army. (26)
The section on the conduct of the commander-in-chief:

[He should be] one born of a noble family, a native of the countryside, skilled in counsel, approved by the ministers, an exponent of the science of government (daṇḍanīti), and a student of it in its true essence. ||27||
Endowed with truthfulness, courage, patience, steadfastness, gentleness, and noble virtues;
possessed of power and energy; and a source of livelihood for those who depend on him. (28)
One who has many friends, is noble and wealthy, has many kinsmen and relatives, is a man of business, is not mean-spirited, and is esteemed by the citizens and the subjects. (29)
He was one who harbored no constant enmities, who committed no harmful acts, whose deeds were followed by auspicious results, who had few enemies, and who was deeply learned. (30)
One who is free from disease, expansive, heroic, generous, a knower of the proper time, endowed with an auspicious appearance, and whose prowess is esteemed by the virtuous. ||31||
Trained in the management of elephants, horses, and chariots, having overcome all fatigue, he was capable of swift movement in sword-fighting and wrestling. (32)
One who knows the divisions of the battlefield, possesses firm prowess like a lion, is not dilatory, is free from lassitude, is indignant at insult, and is not arrogant. (33)
One who correctly knows the characteristics of elephants, horses, chariots, and weapons;
who discerns the differences between men; who is grateful and compassionate. (34)
It is skilled in the application of armor and weapons, follows after what is wholesome, is equipped for all martial activities, and is capable in its training. (35)
He is endowed with the knowledge of the nature of the mind, and he is the knower of horses, men, and elephants, as well as of their names and the means for their training. ||36||
One who knows the nature of local dialects, is skilled in scripts, possesses firm memory, is adept at moving about at night, and is certain in his knowledge of omens; ||37||
He was knowledgeable regarding the rising and setting of the lunar mansions along with the planets,
possessed expertise in the directions, locations, and paths, and was attended by those who knew such matters.
To those who were not afflicted by fear or exhaustion caused by hunger, thirst, fatigue, terror, cold, wind, heat, and rain, he—who was himself agitated by these things—bestowed fearlessness. (39)
A slayer of enemy armies, firm in his resolve even when faced with difficult tasks,
and capable of providing full support to his own troops who have been struck down.
One who considers himself capable of a sudden assault, who understands the operations of an army, who knows the movements of enemy envoys, and who reaps the fruits of great undertakings; 41.
He whose actions were perpetually perfected, who was attended by those whose deeds were accomplished,
who was undaunted in the face of defeats, and who was devoted to the welfare of his illustrious king.
One should appoint as the commander of the army one endowed with such characteristics as these;
being ever-vigilant, he shall protect the army day and night.
Wherever there may be danger— in rivers, mountains, forests, or difficult terrain—
the commander-in-chief shall go to those very places with his forces drawn up in battle array.
The Section on Protecting Against the Calamity of Marching:
The leader should march at the front, surrounded by brave men;
in the middle should be the women, the master, the treasury, and whatever force is weak. (45)
On both flanks were horses; on the flanks of the horses were chariots;
on the flanks of the chariots were elephants; and on the flanks of the elephants was the forest-force.
Thereafter, the skillful commander-in-chief himself, having placed everything in front of him, should march forth with his massed troops ready for battle, slowly comforting those who are weary. (47)
In the face of danger ahead, one should advance with a great crocodile array,
or with a hawk array having its wings raised, or with a needle array called "hero-faced."
When danger is from behind, one should form the cart array (śakaṭavyūha); when from the flanks, the array known as the thunderbolt (vajravyūha);
and when danger is from all sides, one should arrange the all-auspicious array (sarvatobhadravyūha).
Exhausted by the long journey through mountain caves, dense thickets, and the narrow passes of rivers and forests, he was overcome with fatigue from hunger and thirst. (50)
Afflicted by disease, famine, and death, or quickly overrun by bandits;
covered with mud, dust, and water, or scattered and piled up upon the road. (51)
One who is asleep, preoccupied with eating, not on solid ground, or unsteady; one terrified by the fear of thieves or fire; or one overwhelmed by rain and wind. ||52||
When such calamities as these have arisen, one who remains unperturbed should properly protect his own army and strike down the enemy's army. (53)
The Section on the Varieties of Deceitful Warfare:

One who is superior in terms of place and time, whose enemy's constituents are divided, and who is strong, should indeed engage in open warfare; in the opposite case, one should employ deceitful warfare. (54)

At those times of assault, he who stands on firm ground should strike the enemy while they are in confusion and not yet established on their own ground; and he should sow dissension among them regarding that very terrain.

One should strike down those who have been drawn in by the natural capture of forest-dwellers and others with snares, using heroic men through maneuvers that cause a break in their ranks and their extraction. 56.
Having first granted an audience and thereby gained certainty regarding his characteristics, he should subsequently strike him by overwhelming him with a swift and heroic force. //57//
Or, having thrown them into confusion from behind, he should strike them with his core force from the front;
by these two methods, the flanking attacks in deceptive combat are explained. (58)
If the ground is uneven in front, one who possesses speed should strike from behind;
likewise, if it is uneven both in front and behind, or on the two flanks, one should act in the same manner. ||59||
Having first caused the enemy to fight with the forces of traitors, enemies, and forest-dwellers, he—
possessing unwearied mounts— should strike when the foe is exhausted, demoralized, and without support.
Or, having skillfully feigned a retreat by means of the forces of seditious persons or enemies, one who relies on courage should slay the trusting foe, thinking "the victory is already won. (61)
Having enticed the enemy force toward camps, cities, villages, crops, caravans, herds, and the like, he should destroy it while remaining vigilant. (62)
Or, having concealed his strong force with a weak army, he should, like a leaping lion, destroy that [enemy] with little effort when it is vulnerable. (63)
Or he may slay the enemy when he is intent on hunting, having secured his support; or else, by means of a cattle-raid, he may strike him down while he is obstructed on the road. (64)
Out of fear of a sudden assault, he may strike at night when the enemy is exhausted from staying awake,
or during the day when the soldiers are overcome by sleep.
One who is skilled in the methods of a night attack should destroy the exhausted enemy in the afternoon—
either by means of a day-long siege or while they are sleeping in trust at night.
One should carry out the night-attack with nāgas equipped with armor and quivers,
or else with men endowed with fierce speed and swords in hand.
One should strike at the sun's reflection with a great wind while keeping the eyes closed;
in this manner, rising swiftly, one should slay enemies through deceptive combat.
Frost, darkness, charcoal, pits, fire, forests, and rivers—they call these "satra" and so forth; "satra" is proclaimed to be a disguise (chadma). (69)
Being virtuous, vigilant, and resolute in his undertakings,
he should act in such a manner as to destroy the enemy,
having learned the enemy's movements through his spies.
Therefore, being vigilant, one should strike down the enemies with deceptive warfare;
for the slaying of enemies through stratagem does not violate the Dharma. ||70||
The son of Droṇa, with his well-sharpened weapons, slaughtered the army of the Pāṇḍavas at night while they were unawares and fast asleep. (71)
The Twentieth Chapter:
The Section on the Operations of Elephants, Horses, Chariots, and Infantry; marching as the vanguard; and entering a forest-fortress.
And the inauguration of paths and sacred fords that had not been made before. ||1||
Causing the entry [of troops] into water, crossing over [rivers], likewise victory with a single unit, breaking up undivided armies, and gathering those who have been broken; ||2||

The use of intimidation, the destruction of walls and gates, the management of the treasury, the protection against fear, and the employment of elephants—these are declared to be the duties of the army commander. (3)
The deployment of the fourfold army, the protection of forces, the breaking of the unbroken, and the reconciliation of the broken—this is the work of the chariot-warrior. (4)
Searching for forest paths and directions, protecting supplies and reinforcements, pursuing the enemy and withdrawing, and the swift accomplishment of necessary tasks. ||5||
Chasing the weak, striking at the flanks and the rear, and always bearing weapons—this is the duty of the horse and the foot-soldier. (6)
The clearing of wells and sacred bathing places, as well as roads and the camp,
and whatever else such as fodder is to be known— this is the work of forced laborers (*viṣṭikarma*).
Birth, vitality, age, status, life-force, stature, speed, brilliance, skill, loftiness, stability, and being well-disciplined; ||8||

"Excellent in their physical appearance and conduct"—this is the definition for elephants, foot soldiers, and cavalry; one should employ those endowed with these characteristics in their respective duties. (9)
The ground for infantry is considered to be free from large stumps, anthills, trees, shrubs, and thorns; it should have means of retreat and not be excessively uneven. (10)
A horse-course that has few trees or stones, is easily leaped over, free from fear, stable, devoid of gravel, free from mud, and provided with means for escape is excellent. (11)
It was free of stumps, sand, and mud; devoid of anthills and stones;
level; and bereft of fields, creepers, pits, trees, shrubs, and thickets.
Ground that is free from pits, free from fissures, capable of withstanding the treading of hooves, firm, and able to bear the wheels is proclaimed as fit for a chariot. (13)
A terrain where trees are easily crushed, creepers are easy to cut, which is free from mud, and where the unevenness of the mountains is easy to traverse, is known as "elephant ground" (hastibhū).
This earth is not to be approached by them; therefore they are called *nāga* by the wise. For that reason, these grounds are proclaimed as being exceedingly [suitable] for the *nāgas*. (15)
Whatever force accepts horses and other such things when they have been divided is known as "acceptance" (pratigraha); that [force] should be made capable of bearing the burden. ||16||
But that array which is empty of him appears as if it were broken;
therefore, a wise man desiring victory should not fight without a protector.
A king seeking victory should retreat to a distance and accept a challenge;
he should accept one who is divided, for he should not fight with one who is united. (18)
The Section on the Allocation of Gifts:
O King, wherever the virtuous man is mounted upon elephants and attended by swift-footed messengers, there is the treasury; for sovereignty is dependent upon the treasury. (19)
When a deed has been performed, one who praises it and shows respect should then bestow rewards upon the warriors; for who indeed would not fight for a giver? (20)
One should joyfully give a million bharas to the slayer of a king;
half of that for the killing of his son, and likewise for the killing of a general.
For the slaying of a preeminent hero among the foremost warriors, one hundred times a hundred [coins] should be given;
for the slaying of an elephant or a chariot-warrior, half of that amount should be bestowed.

The killing of a horse is declared to be a thousand-fold [fine], the killing of a chief warrior a hundred-fold; for the head [of a criminal] it is twenty-fold, and for the rest, there is a doubling of the fine according to the property involved.
Whatever he wins—the draft animals, gold, or base metals—that belongs to him; or, being delighted, he should gratify the warriors by giving them gifts appropriate to their merit. (24)
The Section on the Array of Formations:
A bow is five cubits long; one should station an archer at that distance in battle.
At three times that distance, a horse should be stationed; at five times that distance, an elephant and a chariot should be joined. (25)
A man [is measured] by an interval of four *śama*s, a horse by three intervals of *śama*s;
an elephant and a chariot are both recorded as being measured by five intervals of *śama*s.
In this manner indeed should the infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants fight,
so that there may be no congestion when retreating from the exertion of battle.
They should fight without confusion, for confusion brings about a chaotic melee;
and in a great battle marked by such confusion, they should take refuge behind great elephants.
Three men should be reckoned as the opponents for a horse;
thus, fifty horses should be assigned to a single elephant. (29)
There are as many foot-guards, fifteen men in total;
this is declared to be the arrangement for the elephant and the chariot. (30)
It should be understood that "anīka" (the array) is to be conceived as nine elephants; and the interval between two elephants in the array is said to be five dhanus. ||31||
Thus, by means of this arrangement of divisions, one should establish the excellence of the battle formation;
these—the breast, the flanks, and the wings—are declared to be equal.
The chest, the flanks, the wings, the center, the back, the reserve, and the two extremities—by those learned in the science of military arrays, this seven-limbed array is prescribed. ||33||
This array, however, with its chest, flanks, and wings, is provided with a reserve;
whereas that of the elder Śukra is devoid of the two flanks. (34)

Those who are indivisible, born of noble lineage, hereditary, skilled in their aim, and capable strikers—such commanders of the army's divisions should be appointed, having been proven in battle. (35)
These should remain surrounded by brave men;
they should fight without breaking ranks and protect one another.
Whatever of the weak troops there may be should be placed in the middle of the array; and whatever equipment for battle there may be should generally be located at its rear. (37)
For the sake of battle, one should employ a troop of shaven-headed men who are skilled in combat;
for battle has the leader as its life-breath, and it would be destroyed if left without a leader. (38)

The array known as "the immovable" (acala) consists of infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants following one another; likewise, it should be understood as "unassailable" when composed of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. //39//
One should place fierce elephants on the chest, chariots on the two flanks, and horses on the two wings; this array is proclaimed as the "breaker of the center. (40)
The division of horses in the center, the division of chariots in the two flanks (kakṣas), and the division of elephants in the two wings—this is known as the "Antarbhid" array. ||41||
One should assign horses to the position of chariots and infantry to the position of horses;
however, in the absence of chariots, one should always employ elephants instead.
Having divided them, one should deploy chariots, infantry, horses, and elephants into the battle array;
if there is an abundance of troops, that is proclaimed as the *āvāpa*.
The wise have proclaimed four types of natural battle arrays (prakṛtivyūha): the circle, the detached, the wealth-array, and the staff; and the variations of these have also been described. ||44||
The horizontal array (daṇḍa) consists of a single line of troops; the extended array (bhoga) is indeed a winding line.
The circular array (maṇḍala) operates on all sides, while the detached array (pṛthagvṛtti) is not concentrated. ||45||
Pradara, Dṛḍhaka, Asahya, Cāpa, and Tatkukṣi; Pratiṣṭha, Supratiṣṭhi, Śyena, Vijaya, and Sañjaya. ||46||
Viśālavijaya, Sūcī, Sthūṇākarṇa, Camūmukha, Jhaṣāsya, and Valaya are the varieties of the Daṇḍavyūha, which are very difficult to conquer.
Having stepped across and stepped back from the two armpits and the sides of the armpits;
having stepped across from the two wings—these three others, however, are the reverse.
Having passed over with the wings and chest, another enters in the reverse order;
there are the pillar-winged, the bow-winged, the double-pillar, the staff, and the upward-moving.
The last [meter] has double [the preceding], while the other has three [syllables] exceeded; in the reverse case, there is another.
These should be known by their characteristics in sequence as "two daṇḍas" and "four daṇḍas. (50)
The *gomūtrikā*, the *ahiśīrṣa*, the *śakaṭa*, and likewise the *makara*—these are declared to be varieties of the *bhoga* (coil), as is the *paripatantika*. ||51||
The *daṇḍapakṣa* (staff-wing) has the yoke as its breast; the *śakaṭa* (cart) is the reverse of that.
The *makara* (crocodile) and the *vyavakīrṇa* (scattered) are the remaining [arrays] formed by elephants and horses.
The two varieties of mandala arrays are the Sarvatobhadra and the Durjaya;
the second consists of eight divisions, while the first faces in all directions.
The *ardhacandraka*, the *uddhāna*, and the *vajra* are the varieties of the *asaṃhata*;
likewise, there are the *karkaṭaśṛṅgī*, the *kākapādī*, and the *godhikā*.

The arrays of three, four, and five troops should be understood according to their different forms; thus have the battle arrays been fully described by those who employ the various types of arrays. (55)
These seventeen types of *daṇḍavyūha* (staff-array) have been described according to their divisions; likewise, there are two types of *maṇḍala* (circle-array) in brief. 56.
The six arrays are uncombined, while the arrays for enjoyment are fivefold;
these should be employed by those skilled in arrays when the time of battle has arrived. (57)
The Section on Open Battle:
Having struck with one side of the formation and so forth, one should surround the enemy with the remaining sides;
or, having struck him with the center, one should encircle him with both flanks. (58)
Having reached the opponent's extremities with both wings along with the grasp, one should strike the groin with the two tips and press it with the chest. (59)
From where it is weak, from where it is divided, and from where it is occupied by traitors—there one should strike the enemy force and thereby strengthen oneself. (60)
One should crush the weak with twice its strength, and the solid with the strong;
one should cause the compact formation to be driven away by fierce elephant divisions.
One should strike down invincible elephants with other elephants drenched in lion-skin fat, or with herds of female elephants well-mounted by riders.
With iron nets, firmly bound teeth, well-constructed, powerful foot-guards,
and heroic warriors whose intoxication was difficult to restrain;
One should destroy the army of enemies with lordly elephants. ||63||
Even a single lordly elephant, endowed with the qualities of rut and courage, destroys the arrayed army of his enemies;
for the victory of kings is established upon their elephants.
Therefore, a king should always possess a force superior to that of an elephant. ||64||
